speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: OPINION OP MR. SPEAKER ON QUESTION RAISED BY MR. J. A. CURRIE.
speechtext:
With reference to the question asked of me yesterday by the hon. member for North Simcoe, I beg to state that the proper manner for the House to express its disapproval with regard to any order passed by the Governor General in Council is to move a humble address to the Crown. The authorities are as follows:
"The subjects upon which addresses are presented are too varied to admit of enumeration. They have comprised every matter of foreign or domestic policy; the administration of justice; the confidence of Parliament in the ministers of the Crown; the expression of congratulation or condolence, and in short, representations upon all points connected with the government and welfare of the country." (iMay, p. 546).
Bourinot is to the same effect, as follows :
"It is now the usage to move for addresses only with respect to matters affecting Imperial interests, the regal prerogative, or the Governor in Council." (Bourinot, p. 2456).
"The subjects on which the two houses may address the sovereign or his representative in this country are too numerous to be detailed at length. They may relate to every matter of public interest, to the administration of justice, to commercial relations, or to the political state of the country; in short, to all subjects connected with the Government and the welfare of the dominions." (Bourinot, p. 259).

speechtext:

Yes. I find in the Journal-Press of to-day, an article reading as follows:
Appointments Within Province.
W. G. McQuarrie, New Westminister, moved an amendment providing that, except as to the city of Ottawa, appointments in any province should, in so far as possible, be made from residents of that province. He said that, within the last few days, application had been made for an additional stenographer in the Government offices at New Westminster. He had been informed that one would have to be sent from Ottawa. He thought his amendment a reasonable one. It would not be advisable, of course, to have all the appointments made in Ottawa from Ontario.
Sir George Foster opposed the amendment on, the score that its tendency would be to cultivate provincialism. The country, he said, should not be cut up into sections. There was no valid reason why a man from British Columbia should not have an opportunity of serving in any part of Canada.
H. H. Stevens (Vancouver Center) said that residents of British Columbia were not afforded proper opportunity to take part in competitive examinations. Owing to the short notice given it was impossible to compete and there were no examinations held in British Columbia at all.
Sir George Foster agreed that there should be equal opportunity given to residents of all the provinces.
Unless there were some safeguards provided, Mr. Cockshutt remarked, all the plums would go to residents of Ottawa and the large cities.
This is the particular part:
Sir Sam Hughes stated that when positions in the Civil Service were vacant they should whenever possible, be filled by men residing in the constituencies in which the vacancy occurs.	-
An amendment to this effect was moved by Mr. Maclean and carried by the House. It had no reference to the inside service.
Mr. iMcQuarrie's amendment stood over.
As a matter of fact, the last part of that report to the effect that the amendment suggested by the hon. member for Victoria (Sir Sam Hughes) was accepted is not correct. I have in Hansard of yesterday the amendment which was finally proposed by the hon. the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Maclean) and adopted. It is this:
Excepting as to the Inside Service, all appointments to any position in a province shall, so far as practicable, be made from bona fide residents of such province.
The point being in regard to the province and not to the constituency as had been suggested by the hon. member for Victoria. The remarkable part of this is that the other paper, the Ottawa Citizen, publishes an exactly similar report in almost the same words. It seems to me a most re-matkable thing that two papers of such
standing as the Citizen and the Journal Press

It is, of course, for the House to determine as to what its desire may be in the premises, but .so far as I am aware there has not been a case where the course asked for in this communication has been followed. The reference to the presence in this Chamber of the President of the American Federation of Labour is hardly in point, because he was the representative of a .great organization in another country. The right Hon. Mr. Balfour, and Mr. Viviani, were also received by this House. In all three oases the privilege was accorded to gentlemen from outside Canada, and it seems to me, with all deference to this organization, that it is a precedent which it may be somewhat dangerous to establish. If I may venture to say so, the receiving of one organization in this country will open the door for similar cases in great numbers to follow. However, I leave the question to the House.

On the order to resume the adjourned debate on the motion of Mr. Maclean (Halifax) for the second reading of Bill No. 87, an Act supplementary to chapter twenty-four of the Statutes of 1917, respecting the Canadian Northern Railway system.

At the conclusion of last night's sitting it was announced that we would proceed to-day with (the Railway Bill, which was to be the first Order of the day. We were prepared to discuss that Bill this morning.
May we not advance this Bill a bit?
I have no objection at all, but that was not the Order which was set down. Yesterday we inquired what was to be taken up to-day, and were told the Railway Bill.

It was the intention to fake up the Railway Bill, but the Acting
Minister of Finance thought it well to advance the Canadian Northern Railway Bill before we proceeded with the Railway Bill.

All right.
On motion of Mr, A. K. Maclean, Bill No. 87 was read the second time, and House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On Section 1-Guarantee on renewal or postponement of payments.

Before this clause carries,
I think the country is entitled to further information on the subject of the Canadian Northern railway. From the statement furnished by the Acting Minister of Finance on Miay 10th, as of September 30, 1917, the total liabilities are shown in round figures as $592,000,000. After deducting from that amount the total capital stock of $100,000,000; the stock of subsidiary companies, some $5,900,000; the reserves of $4,900,000; the affiliated companies advance account of $9,000,000, and the surplus of $34,000,000, there is a balance remaining to be assumed by the country of $437,000,000. According to the statement submitted to the Government by the Drayton-Acworth Commission appointed by the Government to investigate the value and assets of the Canadian Northern railroad, the maximum possible cost of the road would be $370,000,000. From this amount should be deducted the cash subsidies of $38,000,000, the land grant on which cash has been received to the amount of $16,000,000 and land on hand, making a total of $75,000,000. If we deduct this $75,000,000 from $370,000,000, it leaves a balance of $295,000,000 as the total investment in the road, exclusive of the cash subsidies and the land grant. Deducting that amount from $437,000,000 would leave a profit to the promoters of $142,000,000. This road comprises some 9,600 miles, which, divided into the total amount of $437,000,000, would make the cost $46,000 per mile. According to the Drayton-Acworth report, the cost should be $31,000 per mile. In other words, there is a profit to the promoters of $15,000 a mile. Sessional Paper 237, giving a statement of the Canadian Northern railway as o'f June 30, 1916, shows unguaranteed securities at $147,000,000, and from these reports, both the report submitted a few days ago and last year's report, it is apparent that there is a matter of $142,000,000 of promoters' profits.



It may be interesting to the committee and to the country to know if this $147,000,000 of unguaranteed securities represents the amount of water which has been injected into this capital of $142,000,000. The statement last year showed total liabilities of $578,000,000; the statement submitted on May 10 shows liabilities of $592,000,000. The property investment has also been written up $16,000,000 since the last statement was submitted to the House-from $494,000,000, to $510,000,000. No explanation has been offered of what these amounts represent. The committee is entitled to know what are the total assets of the Canadian Northern Railway company, the total assets and liabilities of the subsidiary companies, and the names of the stockholders and holders of securities. Apparently $140,000,000 of the country's money is going to somebody-the people would like to know to whom. We should also be informed who are the holders of the other $8,000,000 or $9,000,000 of common stock. This information has been asked for repeatedly in the House but has never been submitted. In their statement of May 1, 1918, the Canadian Pacific Railway company say:
The total capitalization of the Canadian Pacific Railwav Company's transportation system, comprising 13,400 miles of railway in Canada operated directly by the company, with the rolling stock equipment and steamboat craft on inland waters, its splendid terminal stations and facilities, and other accessories, is $6*3,000.000.
If you divide 13,400 into the amount of capitalization of this company, you find that $46,000 a mile is the cost of the Canadian Pacific railway, containing over one thousand miles of double track, and including terminal facilities, hotels and steamships. We are asked to pay for the Canadian Northern Railway system an amount equal to the capitalization of the Canadian Pacific Railway company. It may be asked how the promoters of the Canadian Northern got this amount of money or these securities above the actual cost of the road. The answer is quite simple. The Government auditors, investigating whether Mackenzie and Mann made any money out of the Canadian Northern, come to the conclusion that they did not. But the auditors did not go as far as the Northern Construction company, which is another Mackenzie and Mann organization. This is the procedure. The Canadian Northern made a contract with Mackenzie and Mann at a certain amount per mile. Mackenzie and Mann let a contract to the Northern Gon-
[Mr. Cahill. 1
struction company at the same price, and the Northern Construction company, in turn do some of the work and let contracts to sub-contractors. The Mackenzie and Mann Northern Construction Company get the profits; the Mackenzie and Mann Construction Company get the common stock-but the Mackenzie and Mann Northern Construction Company and the Mackenzie and Mann Construction Company and the Canadian Northern Railway Company are one and the same people. According to statements furnished by the Government and by the Canadian Northern, they have loaded this enterprise to the extent of $15,000 a mile, practically the cost of the road through the whole prairie section. We are told by the Prime Minister that the Government have safeguarded the interests of the people by appointing their own directors on the directorate of the Canadian Northern. Let me call attention to the names of these Government directors. There is Mr. William K. George, of Toronto, who has been in the Standard SilveT Plating business, and I believe, is somewhat of a political acrobat. Then there is Mr. Graham Bell, an accountant, I understand, in the Civil Service, under the title of financial comptroller-a glorified name for bookkeeper. Then there is Mr. Ediward Rogers Wood of Toronto, who is president of the Central Canada Loan and Savings Company, vice-president of the National Trust Company, vice-president of the Brazilian Traction Light and Power Company, director of the Canadian Bank of Commerce, director of the Toronto Street Railway Company.
He is not a Government director.
My hon. friend has stated that he is.
Mr. Christie, Mr. George and Mr. Bell. '
That is not the information given on Hansard.
Hansard may be wrong.	[DOT]
It should be correct.
The difference is not very serious, anyway.

The difference is not serious, because all the directors now on the directorate of the Canadian Northern Railway Company might be put in a bag and shaken up-and it would not matter which

one the Government put their hand on and named as their director, for they are practically all the same. The information as to the Government directors was given by the Acting Minister of Finance during the course of his statement a few days ago in connection with the Canadian Northern Railway system. If we have no further interest in this enterprise than to appoint such men as these on the board of directors, at least we should, before we vote any further moneys, have a complete statement from the Government as to where these moneys are going and where we expect to end up in connection with this Canadian Northern Railway system. We seem to be getting in deeper all the time. Our liabilities have gone up $13,000,000 to $16,000,000 since last year, on account of this railway system-and the end is not yet. We have not taken over the road; we have not appointed directors who are taking an active part in its management. We are still handing millions to Mackenzie and Mann, and unless we can shake Mackenzie and Mann loose of this proposal the country will not stand for the payment of any further money to it. We should eliminate Mackenzie and Mann from the board of directors, lock stock and barrel, and put in charge men who can manage and operate the road in a businesslike way.. You may say that Mackenzie and Mann are in a better position to manage the road than any new persons coming in. I submit that Mackenzie and Mann built the Toad for the profits that they made out of its construction, and the figures given by the Acting Minister of Finance prove this. Before any further money is voted, the committee should have full information on this subject. The Government have made no statement about what they intend to do in the matter. The question was raised yesterday whether the Government were going to appoint a commission to manage the road, and it was stated that they had formed no plan. Before we make further investment in the enterprise we should form some definite plan of management of the road.

I explained to the House on a previous occasion the purpose of this resolution and of the legislation which is to be based on it. Securities of the Canadian Northern Railway Company mature this year, which they desire to renew, with as small a payment upon principal as possible. That is a businesslike re-
121}
quest, and I cannot understand why there should .be any objection to it. Legislation was passed last year enabling us to make advances to the Canadian Northern Railway Company to an amount not exceeding $25,000,000. .
That amount was disbursed largely in maturity and interest payments. A detailed statement of the expenditures was placed on the table of the House at an early date in the session. Hon. gentlemen will understand that, if the Government can assist the railway in renewing notes or securities maturing during the year, it is in the interest of the road and of the country. My hon. friend wants, some more information. I thought I gave him all the information he could possibly require, and I really do not know of any other information I can give him.
The minister can give the names of the owners of the $9,000,000 worth of stock.
I purpose doing that.

He can also give the names of the owners or pledgees of the securities. He can give the names of the people to whom this money is to be paid, and he can give the whole policy of the Government in regard to this railroad.	.
I do not understand what my hon. friend1 means when he says I might give information as to whom the money wae paid.
The graft money, $25.000,000?
The information with reference to the $25,000,000 is to be found in a return submitted to Parliament.
The return simply gives the name of the subsidiary companies on account of whom it was paid, but not to whom it was paid.
We could get that also.

The return says: Canadian Northern Railway Company, $9,000,000; Canadian Northern Pacific Railway Company, $2,000,000, and so on. It is Canadian Northern right through. The total is $25,000,000, and the dates on which it was paid are November 19, 1917, $12,500,000; November 28, 1917, $2,000,000, and so on down until February 4, 1918, making a total of $25,000,000. Where did this money go to? Who stands between the treasury

and the people who are getting this money, if it is not the minister?

The authority for the payment of the amount referred to by the hon. member is to be found in an Act of Parliament of last year, and the amount was largely expended in respect to securities of the Canadian Northern railway which matured last year.
To whom was it paid?

One cannot tell that. I suppose it is possible to tell who were the holders of the securities and who presented them, but that would be of little information to ihe House. If my hon. friend thinks it is important to him to have that information, I suppose we can get it for him. But these payments were made by the Government, of course, after investigation and audit, and the Government was satisfied that they were obligations which they had authority to pay.
The minister said that the amount was expended largely in the payment of securities maturing. Did it cover them entirely or only in part?
It was expended in paying bonds maturing, interest, equipment notes and some construction work.
We should like to have information in detail in regard to that, how much was for bonds maturing, how much for equipment, how much for interest, how much to banks for commissions.
I shall endeavour to have that on the second reading of the Bill.
We have passed the second reading of the Bill. When shall we have the information?
How many shares has each of the three last named on the list?
Twenty shares each.
Is that what is required by the by-laws?
I assume so.

When was this stock transferred to the Government? When did the Government become the owner of the stock by transfer? That question has been on the Order Paper in various forms, and the date has never been given.

$40,000,000 worth of the capital of the Canadian Northern was in the hands of the Government some two or three years ago. On October 1, 1917, the balance of its holdings was transferred to the Minister of Finance in trust for His Majesty.
Can the minister tell me the standing of the $40,000,000 worth of stock, whether we have acquired that completely, or whether it is still the property of Mackenzie and Mann?
We hold it completely, and have held it for several years.
As security.
No, as proprietors.
Out and out?
Yes.

That is under the old Act.

Mr. DuTREMBLAY: Will the minister give us an idea as to how much money will be required to renew certain of those obligations and on what dates he expects they should be renewed? That would be very important to know.

During the present year?
Mr. DuTREMBLAY: Yes.

We estimate an amount not greater than $6,028,000. That was contained in the statement I gave to the House on Friday last. It is, however, possible that the Canadian Northern railway may be able to renew in full the obligations maturing this year.
Has the Government paid to the Canadian Northern or any of the shareholders thereof any amount on account of the price to be paid for the expropriation of their shares?
No.

In reading the names of the holders of the $9,000,000 worth of shares, I see that they all sound familiar, as being among the directors of the Canadian Northern Railway Company. The names of Mr. Lash, Mr. Christie, and Mr. Horne-Payme were mentioned among others, as being the owners oi the balance of the stock. Why is this $9,000,000 worth of stock not being taken over with the rest?
iMr. A .K. MACLEAN: The Government have authority to acquire it at any time. Section 2 of chapter 24 of the statutes of last year says:
Upon the making of said agreement, at least five-sixths of the said six hundred thousand shares shall be transferred to the Minister of Finance in trust for His Majesty, and if there be any of the said six hundred shares not transferred as aforesaid, the Governor in Council may declare the said shares to be the property of the Minister of Finance in trust for His Majesty, and the same shall thereupon become the property of His Majesty and shall be paid for pro rata with the shares so transferred.
On what basis would that be?
It would depend upon the award made hy the arbitrators.
Why should we let Mackenzie and Mann hold out any of the *stock?

They are not holding it ou't. My hon. friend forgets that this country owns the road. Parliament practically unanimously decided last year to take the road over; I do not think more than two members of Parliament were opposed to it. The only difference of opinion was as to the amount which should be paid for the equity. The road belongs to the people of this country.
The debts.
We are assuming the liabilities. As Parliament almost unanimously adopted last year the policy of taking over the road, vre must, of course, assume the obligations of the road.
Does the minister claim that the Canadian Northern Railway legislation .was put through unanimously last year?
I speak subject to correction, but I think the policy of taking over the road was almost unanimously adopted by Parliament, the only difference being as to the amount paid for the equity.

My recollection is that the
legislation was put through, toy closure.
Not that part.
The whole thing.

If we own the road, why should we not manage it? Why should we leave Mackenzie and Mann and that ring still in control and coming to Parliament for further money? Apparently we own only the liabilities, and we have the privilege of handing out more money. The management of the road is a big business proposition and we should handle it ourselves. The management should have been taken over when the stock was acquired'.
(Mr. BUREAU: They run the country so they might as well run the road.

The Minister of
Finance last year, speaking, about the appointment of a commission or a board to manage the road instead of the present board, said .that the Government thought it advisable to leave the management as it was until the arbitrators made their award. In any event it will not toe long before the Government will have full control of the road. It is undoubtedly a very important matter for deliberation as to how the road shall be managed. I do not know that the interests of the country have suffered by reason of the old directors remaining on the hoard up to the present time. We have representatives on that board.

Is that a statement of the Government's policy, that this same bunch

shall operate the road? The minister says the road is not losing any money.

No. I said that possibly the country's interests were not suffering by reason of the old hoard 'continuing to manage the road. However, it is the intention of the Government to select its own hoard very shortly.

Does not my hon. friend believe that it was the intention of the Government last year to select their own board? Does he not believe that this is the time for the Government to make a statement as to their policy on this very question? We shall have a statement as *to their policy in a very few days, so why not now? If we cannot have it now, why not postpone the Bill? Why put off from day to day the statement of the Government's policy in this matter? These are supposed to be the last days of the session. The Government expects to prorogue this week or next, and in a matter of this importance we are told that we shall have the information some time later. What is the objection to giving the information to the House now? I must say the Government is not treating the House with proper respect. They are not giving us the information which is due to Parliament on this very Bill. We were to have the information, but we have not got it. We were to be informed how this 525,000,000 had been spent, but we have not got that information. This sheet the minister has prepared is not satisfactory; it is not such a statement as we should have. The Government last year determined to acquire the stock of the company, and that stock is ours to-day. The only thing that remains to be done in connection with it is *the fixing of the price, and that matter is now in the hands of the arbitrators. Until the arbitrators have made their award the Government, after acquiring five-sixths of the stock, may make advances to the company. Here is the law:
Upon the making of said agreement, at least five-sixths of the said six hundred thousand shares shall be transferred' to the Minister of Finance.
That stock has already been transferred. Then what takes place?
So soon as the said five-sixths of the said shares have been transferred as aforesaid, the Governor in Council may assist-
Mark the words:
-may assist the Canadian Northern Railway Company, or any company included in the Canadian Northern Railway System, in paying
[iMr. Cahill,]
and settling any indebtedness of such company or postponing the payment thereof on such terms as may be agreed upon, and for such purposes may make advances out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund; Provided, however, that until authorized by Parliament, the total of such advances shall not exceed the sum of twenty-five million dollars.
Mark those words:	The Government

this statement is perfectly justified. May I be permitted to make a suggestion to the minister? This is one of the few Bills which I have seen which has come before the House without a preamble. I should like to have the date inserted in the Bill showing when the last amount of stock, making up the five-sixths, which was transferred to the Government. I would suggest that the following preamble be inserted in the Bill:
Whereas the five-sixths of the shares mentioned in section 3 of chapter 24 of the Statutes of Canada for the year 1917 having been transferred under agreement on the first day of October, 1917, as required by the said Act; therefore His Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows:

Is there a subsequent agreement?

I am not going to offer any remarks on this Bill at the present time because my hon. friend the Minister of Railways (Hon. J. D. Reid) has promised, when he introduces his estimates- and I understand he is going to do it this afternoon-to make a statement to the House which I trust will cover the ground referred to by the right hon. the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier). I want to say to my hon. friend the Acting Minister of Finance that I think he slipped a cog. He is usually very cautious, moderate, and careful in his statements. A moment or two ago he said the country, or at least Parliament, seemed to be anxious and practically unanimous in its desire to acquire the Canadian Northern railway. I did

not understand that that was the position at all. The Canadian Northern and, in fact, all the railways of Canada have been indulging in an orgy for the past twenty or twenty-five years and the people of Canada have been blind to the fact. And now we find the Canadian Northern dumping on the people of Canada against,
I think, the will of the people, this appalling mess-I have thought the words over and I think they -are moderate-a load of $400,000,000 of liabilities that the people have got to shoulder. It is only fair to say that one party is no more responsible for this mess than the other. Both parties have been to- bl-aime, and the people themselves have been to- blame, but we have got to nurse the baby now, and we might just as well -at the start face the issue, which has been dumped upon us.

There is no more milk; we cannot nur-se the baby without milk.
Mr. RI-CHAKDSON:	The milk may be
thoroughly exhausted, ,but here we -are with the system on our hands, and we have got to make the best of it, -although one hon. gentleman -suggests that we should wean the baby. There is no- object in one side of the House indulging in criticism of the other side, because all politicians in the Dominion have been equally responsible for this railway mess, and I repeat that we may just as well make the best of it. I intend to wait until the Government makes its statement before indulging in some comments that I want to make to the House. In the meantime I have some sympathy with those who think that this railway should not be left in the hands of Mackenzie and M-ann and the Canadian Northern directors. Why, all hon. gentlemen need do is to read the press for the last two or three months, and we- find that practically the entire board have overlooked the operation of the road, and they are consumed with eagerness over the arbitration in order that they may bleed the country for the last dollar they can get out of it. After unloading liabilities on this country to the extent of $400,000,000, they -ar-e awaiting results of the arbitration to see whether we cannot give them some more money. The situation is an appalling one, as the Dominion will find very soon, -when i;t undertakes to deal with these enormous liabilities.

An amazing statement has been made to this House by the Acting Minister of Finance, who says that the policy of the Government cannot be given
now, but that it is advisable to withhold it until the -arbitration board now sitting to adjudicate upon the compensation to be paid to the shareholders, has given out its award. Why is this delay taking place? What is the connection between the award of the court now sitting and the administration of the road? And if the gentlemen interested are not satisfied with the judgment which may be Tendered by the board, and take appeal to the Supreme Court, and -from that court to the Privy Council, will we leave these thieves to administer this railway and bleed it in the way they expect to bleed the Canadian treasury by getting the -big award that they anticipate? Will we leave them to bleed the Tailway and bleed this country until the Privy Council has given its judgment?
I think that the hon. member who asked the Government for a definite statement of its policy before entering upon the consideration of this Bill, was justified in his question. The members of the House should not permit the Government to shunt their policy and sidetrack hon. gentlemen and refuse to give them that proper information which we should have before we are asked to give them a blanket authorization to spend money and to renew the liabilities. Before we give such a blanket authorization we should be told what the policy of the Government is to be, and I repeat it, there is no connection whatever between the award of the board of arbitration now sitting and the administration of the road; and if, as the Acting Minister of Finance has just said, the country owns the road, it should -manage it, and not leave the management in the hands of those people who have wrecked the railway after having received from Canada more money than was required to build and operate the system.

I cannot conceive it possible that the remarks made by the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Vien) can possibly have any effect at this juncture in the history of this railw-ay proposition. If I thought that the great Canadian Northern Railway system, which the hon. member fo-r Springfield (Mr. Richardson). calls an abominable mess, was to be left in any uncertain position as to its management, I would certainly feel like withholding this Bill until the Government's policy was declared. I look upon this road as the people's road. It has got to be the people's road and to run independently of the Canadian Pacific railway, or any other large interest. Just here I would like to put a query to the Government,

which they can answer when they like. -whether or not they propose to handle the Canadian Northern system, with its ten or twelve thousand miles of railway, running through a beautiful country in the West and having good connections, a road which brought forty per cent of the grain grown in the West out to the seaports last year, and thirty-three per cent for the last two years; whether they aTe going to run that system as an entity and run it independently, or whether they are going to link it up with the existing Government Railway 'systems? I think the country ought to know that. I think the country ought also to know the principle upon which the Government intend to operate the Canadian Northern system, which, to my mind, should be operated in the meantime independently of other Government roads, until it is put into the position where the publio will be able to ascertain the facts', both as to the condition of the roadbed, and the value of the holdings, and determine what the future policy ought to Ibe. Personally, I am not a pessimist in regard to this great railway. There may have been mistakes made in its administration in the past, but I believe it will yet be a great asset to the country. I have been over the system, I have looked at it with independent eyes, and have ascertained from personal observation that the most fertile country in the world, from an agricultural point of view, is served by this road. The Canadian Northern system has built up large sections of the West, and I look upon it with a great deal of hope in connection with the development of the country. It will be a great asset, and I am not going to deny to Mackenzie and Mann the courage and the vision they had-and the courage and vision of those who assisted them-when this road was built. I believe that there has been a mistake made in our railway policy. That mistake, however, did not lie m the Canadian Northern, but in the duplication of railways by the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Transcontinental. I want to ask the Government whether this railway is going to foe really a people's road, and whether their policy will have the effect of eliminating political influence from it? Will there be an independent board-which I submit there should foe; an independent entity from the Railway Commission, presided over by either a strong railway man, or a man who has had to do largely with railway legislation, litigation, operation and work, whether in a real opera-
five capacity, or as having had to do with large affairs through parliamentary life? Because herein lies the principle that can safeguard the situation. And in speaking of that, I come right back to the place which the road occupies: the Canadian Northern will be a competitor in the public interest with every other large railway corporation, both on this side of the international boundary line and on the other. This road will be a competitor to the Canadian Pacific railway. I hope the Government will not in any way relax their view of the people's interest by appointing a board which will be subservient to pressure from the Canadian Pacific railway. I think the safety valve for the future public interest in railway matters will be an absolutely non-political and independent board of administration. May I suggest to the Government what I think would be the proper basis? We have asked-I have not myself, but I have heard it asked four or five times this morning-if the Government have a policy and what is their policy.
We have all asked that.

I have heard it asked. We have had no answer. If the Government were prepared to say that they had not framed a policy, that would be an answer, and the natural reply to that would be that this Bill should not pass until the Government gave the House some idea of its policy. My idea of the way to run this road-and it seems probably presumptuous that a man should set up his idea, but I think that constructive criticism is fair criticism-would be to adopt the principle applied on the Suez canal. That principle was international, and was based on what ought to be the charge for tonnage passing through it. The charge at first was ten francs per net ton. In 1869 there were three million dollars collected in tolls on tonnage passing through the Suez canal; in 1916 there was over sixteen million dollars in tolls. The object in running that canal has always been to reduce rates. From 10 francs, the rate came down to 7f francs' at one time; then it went back to 8|. But the law-it is the French company law that administers the canal-provides that if the percentage of profit reaches 25 per cent, the surtax on rates which they have applied in the principle of operation shall be reduced until it is wiped out, and ultimately it is hoped that the rates will be reduced to 5 francs per ton. That is a real principle which has been operated by an administra-

tive board of thirty-two, ten of whom are English appointees, because the English tonnage and interest are very large on the Suez canal. Such a large board would be very cumbersome, no doubt, here. The reason it is so large, to my mind, is that there are so many countries interested that they must have representation.
I would not fix such a large board for Canada, but that principle should be applied here so that this system can be and shall be worked independently by the Government through an administrative council or independent board, which will have but one thing always in its eye, the reduction of rates, consistent with proper maintenance and expansion by branch lines, and so on. The public interest is in reduction of rates, both for the farmer in the West and for the industrial man in the East. I do not take very much stock in the cry about Mackenzie and Mann; I do not believe the Government are guilty of anything wrong in the fact that their name has to come up in this House, because I thoroughly believe that financially and so far as the management is concerned, they have been eliminated entirely, and that the Government have a free hand, as free as the air, in dealing with this railway. What I complain of is that the Government have not let the country know their policy; they have brought themselves under some opprobrium by creating, for lack of giving information, a suspicion that Mackenzie and Mann do own the Government. That is not so, and I do not believe it. But the sooner we get a statement of the Government's policy and the form the administration of the railway will take the sooner will the country's mind be settled and satisfaction will reign, particularly if such principles are applied in the railway policy as will result in a reduction of rates, by competition if necessary.

The hon. member for Lotbiniexe (Mr. Vien) a few moments ago made the statement, if I understood him correctly, that no information had been given as to when there would be a change in the directorate of the Oanadian Northern railway.
If the hon. minister will let me correct him, I said that the Government did not give any information as to the policy they intended to follow in the administration of the road.

A few days ago the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson) complained as to there not having been a change in the directorate of the Canadian Northern since the transfer of the stock in October last. I replied to that hon. member that a change in the directorate would take place as soon as the arbitra-torsi' award had been made. I think he raised the question that perhaps the award might be appealed to the Supreme Court and then to the Privy Council, and that it might be a year or two' before a final decision was arrived at. I replied that there would be no time lost after the award, that even if there was an appeal a change in the directorate and a reorganization would take place.
What is the reason for waiting until that award is made?

I might say to the hon. member that the Prime Minister explained the reason *a few days ago in the House. The reason, as I understood him then, and as we all understood, was that at the time the Canadian Northern was transferred, it was understood that the organization of the directors would remain as it was until the arbitrators' award had been made.
Understood between whom?

At that time we did rot think it would take so long, we expected that the arbitration would have taken only two or three months and would have been over long ago. Complaint has been made several times this morning that the railway policy of the Government has not been given to the House before.
(Mr. LEMJEUX: Why not give it this afternoon when the farmers are here?
Let me say to the hon. member that this is really the first opportunity that we have had. We have not been on any railway estimate yet.
Yet you want to close the session on Saturday?
I would say to hon. members that if the Prime Minister had not been engaged at the meeting with the farmers this morning he would, no doubt, have announced the railway policy.
Then my hon. friend cannot make the announcement in the absence of the Prime Minister?

The reason it is hardly fair to ask me is that it has been asked to give the policy for the whole Canadian railway system. I am dealing entirely with the Oanadian Northern system, and the

Prime Minister is the person upon whom the duty of giving the whole railway policy of Canada devolves.
Will he give it this afternoon?

The Prime Minister will be here. So far as the operation of the Canadian Northern is concerned, some hon. gentlemen have asked what the intention of the Government is: Will it be operated as a separate system; will the other Government railways be kept separate from it; will political patronage be kept out of it? I think I made a statement here a few days ago that the Canadian Northern Railway system is a separate corporation. It is' the intention of the Government to see that the operation of the Canadian Northern is carried on free from patronage in any shape or form. In its operation it will be kept as far from the Department of Railways as possible. We will re-organize the board of directors, the members of which, in respect of future operations of the Canadian Northern, will be selected by the Government.
Is the board to be elected by the shareholders under the charter of the company, or does the Government propose to institute a form of administrative council entirely apart from that?

The directors would be selected under their charter by the shareholders of the company, being the nominees of the Government. I do not see the difference between naming a body as a board of directors and appointing a separate commission.
Can you organize a new system without legislation?

It is not necessary to
organize a new system'. You can appoint directors who would have the same powers as a Government-appointed commission. Of course, the Government must be responsible for the men they name as directors. Every charter specifies the length of time during which the board of directors shall operate. It does not make any difference, whether we appoint this body as a board of directors or as a commission.
It has been asked whether the Government intend to operate the Canadian Northern railway system separate from the Canadian Government railways. My own opinion is that, so far as possible, the Canadian Northern railway and all roads owned by the Government should be tied

up together and operated as cheaply as possible. It is my view that any railways that we own should be put under the same management as that of the Canadian Northern Railway system-under a commission, if you wish to call it that, or a board of directors. Why should the terminals of the Government railways and the Canadian Northern at Winnipeg be operated by two separate staffs? 'Why should they not be operated under one system? Why should not the same apply to other terminals throughout the country? Why should not the two roads running between Winnipeg and Quebec, one the Government-owned road and the other the Canadian Northern-the latter owned by the Government through the stock-he under one management in the matter of operation, but, in their relation to the department, as distant as the poles so far as political patronage is concerned? That is the way I feel about it. When the matter is taken up and discussed in Council, that is the position I shall take as a member of the Government.
Does the minister say that the matter has not yet been taken up by the Cabinet?

We have not taken it up as to the personnel of the new board; the time for that will not have arrived until we have reorganized the board of directors. The present directors and their officials are operating the road in the interests of the country. They are not permitted to spend any money in new works or to make any abnormal expenditures' without the sanction of the Department of Railways and Canals. In other words, they are operating the road with the least possible expense, pending the reorganization of the board. I feel that it would be much better if we did not do away with the identity of t'he Canadian Northern Railway system at the present time. The Government must go out to the markets of the world and renew the securities that are now falling due. We may have to borrow more money on the system, and, if we do, it may be necessary to raise money on bonds and securities of the Canadian Northern, which the Government must endorse. It would not make good reading for those to whom we apply for loans if expressions of opinion should go out indicating that members of the House have not the same confidence in the noad that, perhaps, the Government have. The impression that might be conveyed is that

the whole off the $400,000,000, representing the expenditures on the road, have been squandered. I have great confidence in the future of the Canadian Northern Railway system. Expressing my own private opinion, I believe that that system in years to come will prove to be one of Canada's greatest assets. Having Tegard to the $400,000,000, it is to be remembered that the construction of the Canadian Northern throughout the Northwest and in other parts of Canada has enormously increased the value of the lands and property through which it runs-practically to the extent of half the value of the road. This system is virtually bringing into the country $200,000,000 or $300,000,000 a year in the products that are raised in the vicinity of its lines. This the country would not have had if the Canadian Northern Railway system had not been constructed.
Or some other system.

If the Canadian
Northern system had not been promoted and carried on by those who constructed it I doubt whether other systems would have done the same work. Certainly they would not have done so without coming to this Parliament and getting the financial assistance that the Canadian Northern got.
Is it the policy of the Government to acquire any of the other railway systems in Canada?

I do not wish to be unfair to the hon. member, but he has asked me a question that I would like him to leave until the Prime Minister gives a statement in regard to the whole railway question. The hon. member has asked me to go outside of the Canadian Northern Railway system at the present time. I stated a minute or two ago that I would like that to be left until the Prime Minister makes to the House the statement that was promised at the time we went into the railway estimates. By the way, the right hon. leader of the Opposition a few minutes ago raised the question as to why we did not take up the Railway Bill this morning. Some of the hon. members say that they may have to. leave soon. We thought it would probably be better, before we took up the Railway Bill, to have a statement on the whole railway question, and for that reason I intended, if we had got through with this matter, to have seen the Prime Minister and perhaps have that statement made this afternoon, and then we could go on with the Railway Bill.
An excellent intention.

This is, as I stated a few minutes ago, the first opportunity we had, and, therefore, I do not think there is any fault to be found at the present time. I think I have answered the hon. member for North Perth (Mr. Morphy), and the hon. member for Lotbinifere (Mr. Vien). If not,
I shall be very glad to give any further information.

I shall again put my question, because I do not think the minister has answered it. I asked why the Government was waiting, before determining upon its policy, until the award was given by the Court now sitting in arbitration upon the Canadian Northern. The minister has replied that, because an agreement was entered into between the Government and the managers of the railway, those managers would continue to administer the affairs of the railway until the award was given. That is no answer. That is no reason. Why was such an agreement entered into? Why did the Government enter into an agreement with the managers of the road to leave them in charge of the road until the award was given? The Government becomes the owner of the road and yet leaves the management of the road to persons who have no longer an interest in it. Will the minister kindly tell us the reason for making such an arrangement?
I am sure, if the hon. member considers for a moment, he will see the unfairness of his statement.
I do not see it.

Supposing the hon.
member was entering into an agreement to buy a piece of property, he surely would not expect to take possession of the property without even paying for it or saying what he will pay for it. We cannot take possession until the arbitrators come to some final decision. The agreement was made.

The minister knows perfectly well that the moment the Government expropriates a thing, that thing is vested in the Crown by the mere expropriation of it, and the Crown takes immediate possession before the award is given. When the Crown, for any public purpose, expropriates land, it takes immediate possession. The land is vested in the Crown, and the owner has no longer anything to do with it.

The hon. member, who, I understand, is a lawyer, knows the differ-

ence between expropriation and agreement. He has read this Bill. He knows that we did not expropriate the railway.
The Government cannot get away from the Bill.

We have not expropriated the railway at all; we have taken it on an agreement, and we are going to carry out that agreement. The agreement is that we are going to take a transfer of the road, have the ownership in our name, and take over the absolute reorganization of the board of directors as soon as the final award is made.
Where is that in the statute?

What is the reason for that agreement? What reasonable ground is there for waiting for the award /before taking over the management of the road? I cannot get an answer. What is the reason? Why is the Government waiting? I cannot get any answer to that.

Did I understand the minister to say that, as soon as the award is given by the arbitrators, the Government will take control of the road? There was an objection raised as to that, that the award might be carried to the Supreme Court or to the Privy Council. The minister said that would not make any difference, that the moment the award was given, reorganization would take place.
That is what I said.

Then the minister says the Government cannot take over its property until it is paid for, and it cannot be paid for until the price has been settled by some tribunal. The minister answers himself. He destroys the reason that he gives. If the Government is to take over the road after the first tribunal has given its award, the Government does not know what it is going to pay. The award may be reversed or modified by the Supreme Court. The reason given by the minister does not stand, and if that is the reason, it is no explanation to the hon. member for Lot-biniere (Mr. Vien).

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the section pass?
No.

Certainly not. The matter was opaque when the Acting Minister of Finance got through with it; it is now further obscured by the verbal fog which has been raised by the Minister of Railways, and which it will take all the in-
TMr. J. D. Reid.]
genuity of the Government to dispel. The question that has been asked is a perfectly proper one, one that suggests itself to the minds of those who were members of the last Parliament, perhaps more readily than to the minds of those who are members of the new Parliament, although our new colleagues must be asking themselves the same question-why do the Government not take over the management of the road? Just for a moment let us look at what has happened- The Minister of Railways and Canals in one breath speaks of a statute under which it was provided to take over the stock of this company, and in the next he says that there was an agreement, thereby conveying, possibly not with the intention of misleading any one, an intimation that at the same time as the statute was enacted, an agreement was made or was embodied in the statute that the management was not to be taken over until the award was made and the amount paid. There never was any such agreement. Had such an agreement been mentioned at the last session, when this Act was under consideration, not even closure would have succeeded in getting that Act passed. There was no intimation that there was any such agreement. If anything of that kind has been done, then it has been done outside of the terms of the statute passed, at the last session; it has been done without the authority of Parliament. What is going on at the present time by reason of the road not being taken over and by reason of the Mackenzie and Mann organization being left in charge of affairs just as they were last year? This is what is going on. This is the spectacle that is being presented to this country. An arbitration is taking place in the city of Toronto, the parties to the arbitration being on the one side the gentlemen that are interested in this road, and the parties presumed to be on the other side, the people of Canada, represented by this Government. By the fact that Mackenzie and Mann are Left in charge of the organization, the people's side is being presented: by Mackenzie and Mann. That is what is happening. There is no adjudication; there is no litigation being carried on with parties on opposite sides, with opposing interests, with their interests being represented through different counsel and so on. That is not being done. Mackenzie and Mann are left in charge of the situation. They are in charge of the books and records and all the information connected with this road. The people's interest's are not being conserved or properly presented

before this Board of Arbitrators, and this committee is entitled to know whether that is the reason why the management of this road has not been taken over by the Government. Is it because the Government are willing that all the information should remain in the hands of Mackenzie and Mann, that the people's case might be either improperly presented or not presented at all before that board of arbitrators, so that Mackenzie and Mann would get an award to which they would not be entitled if the people's case were properly presented? If the Government were in charge of this road and had possession of all the records of the company and knew all the details and ramifications of the workings of that organization, the people's case could be properly presented before the board.

The Government's
counsel, Mr. Tilley, had free access to all the books of the company and to all the officials of the company. They furnished him with all the information it was possible to get concerning the Canadian Northern railway. The whole Canadian Northern organization was working with him, that he might present his case to the arbitrators in the fullest possible manner.

I have the greatest possible respect for Mr. Tilley; I have great admiration for his legal ability, but that does not alter what I am saying or affect the situation in the slightest degree. The people's case, I maintain, is not being presented before that board of arbitration as it should be, and it is not being presented as it should be for the reason that the Government has not taken possession of the road and of the books and records of the company, showing all the details of the workings of that organization. Everybody who has had anything to do with the proceedings of the' board of arbitration speaks of the situation in exactly the same terms as those I am now using.

FORMATION OF FRENCH BRIG AIDE ADVOCATED BY MR. DuTHBMBLiAY.
On the motion of Hon. A. K. Maclean (Acting Minister of Finance) for the House to go into committee of supply:
Mr. P. R. D uTREMBLA Y (Laurier-Outremont): Mr. Speaker, before the House goes into committee of supply, I would like to put before it a question which is considered of very great importance and that is the desirability and propriety of forming a French Canadian brigade for overseas service, commanded by officer® speaking the French language. In the province from which I come this question is considered as being of paramount importance and as one affecting the best interests of the country. That is why I ask the indulgence of the House while I briefly present the reasons for the request which I shall make to the Government. I submit that the number of French-Canadian soldiers actually at the front, together with those who are in England and those who will be enlisted under conscription, will be sufficient to justify the organization of a French Canadian brigade; and therefore I -strongly urge upon the Government to take this matter into their immediate and favourable consideration. As you are aware, Mr. Speaker, a brigade is composed of four regiments, or battalions, of 1,000 men each. There are actually, from the province of Quebec, seven regiments of which only one regiment is composed entirely of French Canadians and commanded by officers speaking the French language. The other six regiments are English regiments and are commanded by English speaking officers. The recruits that go from the province of Quebec to England are sent to a single unit depot and from that depot the seven regiments at the front secure the drafts necessary to keep their ranks filled. Whether they are English or French Canadians they draw from that unit depot all the soldiers they need. A few weeks ago a regiment in England composed entirely of French Canadians, the 150th Regiment, was disbanded. That regiment was commanded by a very competent and brave officer, who organized a regiment in Canada at the beginning of the war; he had been

in France* had been wounded, came back tQ Canada, raised another regiment, and went with it to England. That is the regiment which has now been disbanded. Four hundred of the French Canadian members of this regiment were merged into English regiments from the province of Quebec. Only 100 of these men remained to fill the ranks of the 22nd, which is the French Canadian regiment commanded by French officers.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Did the hon. gentleman say the 107th regiment?
Mr. DuTREMiBLAY: The 150th regiment commanded! by 'Col. Barre.
Sir SiAM HUGHES: It was in the 5th division.
iMr. DuTREMiBLAY: I would like to put before the House a copy of a letter that was sent by Col. Barre to Sir Edward Kemp, Minister of the Overseas Military Forces. It gives certain reasons why the French Canadians should be grouped together in their own battalions and I think it would help my request if I put this letter before the House. It is as follows:
Witley, Surrey, February 14th, 1918. Sir Edward Kemp,
Minister of the Overseas Military Forces, London.
Sir,-
If I take the liberty of writing' you this letter, it is not to protest against the military decisions or plead my personal case, but I have in view the prevention of a wrong to .my men which is as useless as undeserved. It is therefore with confidence in your sense of fairplay and in the justice of niy case, that I submit to you the following:-Canadian Headquarters have ordered the 150th Canadian Infantry Battalion to be broken up and its effectives disposed of in a certain way. I am convinced that this step, and the trend it exhibits, constitute a grievous error. And I would be remiss in my clear duty if I did not put forward certain considerations -which militate against that step being taken.
If it had been intended to punish me and my battalion for a breach of discipline, no more drastic measure could have been adopted than the order to break it up and disperse its men, without their Officers, through the cadres of four different English speaking battalions.
I am now under orders to draft out five hundred men. Of these, only one hundred are to go to the only French Canadian battalion in the fighting line; the rest are to be posted to English Canadian units from the province of Quebec. Even if the necessity of breaking the cadre were conceded, from every point of view, the dispersion of the men is indefensible. The great majority of my command have a very poor command of English. As a direct consequence, many of them will have to carry out, and risk punishment for inadequately carrying out orders, the full1 purport of which they cannot gather. I urge upon you that this
IMr. DuTremblay.I
would work actual injustice, to say nothing of the resulting inefficiency.
Either the English Canadian battalions from Quebec have exhausted their proper recruiting sources, i.e., the English speaking population of the province, or they have not. If they have not, there can be no necessity for supplying them from other sources. If they have, they should be gradually withdrawn from the line and broken up to supply the remaining battalions fed from the same source. The only escape from this dilemma, under the territorial supply establishment, is by invoking sentimental reasons.
Now, on sentimental grounds the breaking up of my battalion is open to question. The proposed dispersion of its effectives is still more questionable. It can be proven, and after the war is over it will be, proven that the provision of inadequate distinctive cadres for such French Canadians as offered to enlist was a potent check on recruiting from that element in Quebec. When French Canadian battalions were authorized, recruiting picked1 up somewhat but was again severely checked when unit after unit was broken up after arrival in England and their effectives dispersed through several different battalions. I noticed an immediate decline in voluntary enlistment when this was first done. A similar and proportional cooling off has followed the successive dissolution of French Canadian units until recruiting sank to zero.
At present, French Canadian minds are rather exasperated. It is not for me to seek the responsibility for their attitude. It is sufficient to note it as a fact, and to draw attention to it as a factor. Is it wise to furnish fuel to the incendiaries of public opinion in the province of Quebec, who will not fail to point out that this dispersion is like that of the Acadians, that it is made in pursuance of a determination to shed French Canadian blood without credit to the French Canadians, that it is dictated by a resentment of the recent vote cast by the province on the issue of conscription, and so forth?
May I suggest that if, as I am assured is the fact, the 1st Quebec Regiment and B. C. Reserves are not in a position to carry the burden of six battalions each at the front, the situation could be remedied by placing my battalion in the fighting line instead of a Montreal or British Columbia battalion on the point of growing too weak. This reasonable increase of French Canadian cadres would provide a reasonable and pleasant outlet for the French Canadian conscripts.
If this is too much to grant, might the battalion be drafted by companies, to which French Canadian conscripts could1 afterwards be sent, thus avoiding the injustice and inefficiency to which I have already drawn attention as resulting from lingual differences? I believe that this has been done in the case of one battalion ordered to be broken up.
This appeal to you is made with the greatest certitude that it shall have your serious consideration and dealt with the high spirit of justice and diplomacy which an officer who has been doing his duty since the first day of the war, can expect from his Minister of Militia.
This letter is signed by Hercule Barre, LieutenantnColonel 150th Canadian Infantry Battalion. A similar letter was sent to

Sir George Perley, and to Baron Beaver-brook, but without any result.
A few weeks afterwards this battalion was disbanded and merged into English battalions. Now, Mr. Speaker, I lay down the principle that it is necessary to group French Canadians together for >a strong Teason which does not exist in the case of the men from the- English-speaking provinces, namely, because of their speaking and understanding best the French language. Most of the French Canadians do not speak, and do not understand English;
I know that English battalions from some of t!he other provinces were disbanded and broken up upop their arrival in England, just as was done with a number of battalions, or regiments, that came from Quebec. But the language difficulty which necessitates preserving intact the French Canadian regiment, does not exist in the case of the English-speaking battalions. I!f it is desired to secure to the fullest extent that discipline and that esprit de corps thai is essential in all regiments and in all armies, and to achieve success in military measures, men from the same city, or from the same village, must be placed together. This principle, or what is called the territorial idea, is not new. It exists in France and in Switzerland, and it was accepted by Lord Roberts, and afterwards by Lord Kitchener. It is a principle of general acceptance, that men from the same village should be formed into a company, and men from the same district into a Tegiment, where their numbers permit. It is necessary when these men are at the front that pride of race and pride in their regiment should be aroused in them to such an extent that they are prepared to die, if need be, for the honour and glory of their flag.
The French Canadians come of a rade that appreciate to the utmost what is meant by courage, honour, and sacrifice. In speaking thus, I do not wish to reflect on the other nationalities of 'this country, whose qualities I admire and recognize, but I am speaking now on behalf of my own people. The people of Quebec know full well the history of such famous regiments as the Legion Etrangere, the Turcos, the Zouaves, and the Alpines, whose bravery is renowned the world over, and whose regimental flags have been decorated time after time by the Government of France. They know, too, that it Is the greatest punishment and the greatest dishonour for a regiment to be debarred from attacking or defending [DOT] a position of danger. And what
has developed those ideals? It is the esprit de corps which prevails in those historic battalions and the desire to perpetuate their glory. Therefore, if we are to have amongst the sons of Quqbec the highest efficiency, if it is desired to treat justly, the men of my race, the suggestion which I am making should be given effect to by the Government. The desirability for forming a French Canadian brigade is fully concurred in by the people of Quebec. Nearly all the men -who have been closely identified with recruiting in my province, and almost all the newspapers, are in favour of this scheme, and I submit in this connection a splendid patriotic article which I read in Le Devoir a few days ago. I have translated this article, though I am afraid the translation will not do it justice. It is as follows:
For our Conscripts.
Our young- men have come by hundreds to enlist during the last few days. Considerable groups have already voluntarily enlisted in the Flying Corps and in other dangerous services. They will go bravely. All will do their duty, as did the boys of the 22nd Battalion.
General Mewburn, Minister of Militia, noted specially the conduct of these boys, some days ago, and declared himself sympathetic with the idea of grouping them as much as possible from the start, and of keeping them together [DOT] also on the battlefield. That would indeed be an excellent means to keep up their esprit de corps ; it will encourage them if they are merged in one combatant unit, so that they will not feel themselves too far away from their country, and alone in a strange land. This is well understood in the English military centres. An English catholic chaplain, the Rev. Father O'Gorman, according to a despatch from London published by the Globe, wrote to the Times on the 15th of April as follows : "That it was urgent to increase the number of French Canadian battalions in France." This opinion comes at the proper time, now that thousands of our French Canadians entering under the conscription law, or voluntarily, are preparing themselves to go across the sea.
To give them officers of their own blood and language would be equally an excellent measure. The Gazette correspondent in London said the other day, on the- occasion of the merging of the 150th French Canadian regiment with an English regiment, that it was regrettable that these men had not been merged in a regiment commanded by Quebec officers. The Toronto News the other day was scandalized and astounded because certain Austrian soldiers had German officers to command them; so that newspaper will now understand the attitude of its English confrere and also the good sense of the words in the Star the other day, of Rev. Father Doyon, military chaplain, who said in London, on May 1st: "All that we desire is that the French Canadians as much as possible shall stay together and have officers speaking the French language."
It is also time to consider the question of the
formation of a French Canadian brigade to



form part of the Canadian divisions in France. For a long time, this project has been before the people without any result; circumstances were against it; it would appear also that it had the hostility of the .higher functionaries. But, as the project* of putting French Canadian conscripts in regiments commanded by officers speaking their language is highly commendable, the more ambitious project of forming a brigade of our men to be commanded by a general from our province should also appeal to the military authorities, if they are looking first and foremost to the best way of putting -their conscripts in the best frame of mind before sending them to the front.
One of our European correspondents, well informed as to what is going on in the Canadian camps in England and in France, wrote us this authentic fact:	" At Witley, a boy from
Quebec province, being ridiculed, badly treated and unable to obtain his transfer from the Ontario Artillery to another unit where he could speak French and be well treated, committed suicide in a moment of despair." It would not be right to put our conscripts in such a position and expose them to such a temptation.
So we hope that General Mewburn, who seems to have good intentions, if he desires to be just, will take the necessary steps at London for the welfare of the French Canadians in ' the army. It is surprising also, -as someone said, that it is at London and not at Ottawa that these details are settled. But, whatever the reason may be it is the duty of the military authorities to see that our conscripts are in charge of officers coming from their province.
These men are going on the battlefield. Numbers of them will meet death. They will fight with courage and with valour, and will prove to those who discredited them that they are not cowards and that what has kept them here far from the European front, were highly respectable motives. Surely, they have the right, at this supreme hour, to hear the language of their land to encourage them to go through fire and death; and we cannot refuse them at this last moment the right of French Canadian comrades to surround them, help them, and receive from their dying lips the last message to their families who are far away.
May it be that on the soil of France, these brave men will have the impression that they are fighting not among strangers but among friends and comrades who will recall to them their native land.
There is another article from L'Evene-ment, a Quebec organ friendly to the Government, of the same tenor as that I have read from Le Devoir, asking that a French Canadian bridgade be organized. I would also read to the House a letter sent to me by Colonel Mignault, who is well-known to the military authorities in Ottawa, who helped to organize the 22nd Battalion, who also organized the French Canadian hospital unit in France, .actually operating in France to-day in St. Cloud. The letter says:
Montreal, April 29th, 1918.
P. R. duTremblay, M.P.,
House of Commons.
Ottawa.
Dear Sir,
Referring to our recent conversation with reference to the drafting of the French Can-

adians into the English regiments, I have consulted with friends of prominence down here who understand the situation, and we feel most strongly that it is our duty to ask you to lay before the authorities the justice of the claim of the French Canadians to a brigade of their own at the front, or failing this, at least a new battalion. If only on the score of the more efficient work that will be derived having the French Canadians under officers speaking their own language, the request, should commend itself, and as we are all working for a speedy and successful termination of the war, this argument would seem unanswerable. The sentimental aspect of the situation also is a very important one, as it is known that to-day the French Canadian recruits, as well as going to the 22nd Battalion, are also sent to the 5th C.M.R., the 13th, 14th, 24th, 87th and 42nd.
It is a simple calculation for the authorities to see how, with conscription, a French Canadian brigade could now be kept up, and the English regiments should, as has been done in the past, if they cannot keep up their own reserves, be merged.
Can anyone in fairness be asked to risk his life and the life of many others in taking instructions in a language he does not understand? This must happen in the near future if the present policy is continued. I could write much more on this subject, but as we have discussed it very fully, I must leave it to you to place before Parliament this most important and vital question to our people.
Of course, as I have already mentioned to you in our previous interview, it has always been, and still is to-day, my ideal that all French Canadians should be sent to the French Army.
Very truly yours,
Arthur Mignault.
This question of putting French Canadians in the French army has been discussed	before. I	know it	was
discussed with the President of France. The Prime Minister had an interview on the subject with Colonel Mignault. I understand that the Prime Minister, if not in favour of the suggestion, -was at least inclined to look upon it as a, good one. For one reason or another, however, the matter was dropped, and we did not hear any more about it.
In this connection I want to read a letter from a gentleman in Montreal who has done good service in the cause of French Canadian recruiting:
May'2nd, 1918.
My dear DuTremblay:
Having, as you know, taken a great interest in the French Canadian recruiting ever since the war started, having been one of the organizers of the 22nd., 41st. and other Battalions, to the 22nd, (I sent over six hundred men from this district), and being also a member, appointed by the Government, of the French Canadian Recruiting Committee, I write to you, as a member representing one of the largest French and English constituencies of our City.
I would like to bring your attention very

strongly to your duty, as pointed out by myself and the gentlemen that met you recently, of how necessary it is that the Government at once announce a strong policy of giving to these French Canadians, officers of their own, speaking their own language, and promise another French Canadian regiment at the front at once, with a French brigade in the near future, a wonderful step forward will be made. The fullest publicity of the French press, however, should be given to this. The whole situation has, however, been explained to you by French Canadians who have the welfare of their people at heart, military men and others. You, therefore, should be well posted and, apart from the justice of the claim, can lay the facts before the House, so that every fair minded man will understand the situation. It should be quite clear that a French Canadian, not speaking a word of English, cannot in a short time before he is sent into the firing line hope to learn enough English to understand the difficult explanations that he will need to be given, nor can be bring back and give in English the information he will gather. We understand that the authorities on the other side have many important questions at present to settle, and as they are over there in charge should be interfered with as little as possible, but in this case do they understand the present position and situation in the province of Quebec, and can they view it as we do? I think not, as otherwise there should be no hesitation in, at once, granting the French Canadians what they ask. The record of the 22nd needs no comment and, as you are aware, their commanding officer, Colonel Tremblay, a Kingston graduate, has a splendid record. He has, under him, officers who have been there since the beginning of the war, whose records, we understand1, are of the best. Surely, in the question of the formation of a brigade. Colonel Tremblay could be asked if this could be done. He has the welfare of his people and his men at heart. This is only a suggestion, but might be brought forward, as I see by the press that the claim is made that there is no material for a brigade. With the recruiting that is now going on of the French Canadians, and taking the percentage of wastage at 2,500' a year for each battalion, this statement cannot stand. Sufficient reinforcements from this province can easily go forward to maintain a brigade, and if a school for young officers is formed in this province, a wonderful stride forward in the development of the situation will be made. Look into the enlistment of the young men, of French Canadians that have gone into the Flying Corps and the Tank Battalion in the last month, and you will see that now that conscription is the law it is going to be obeyed, but please do not hesitate to show the Government that the people of this province must be given men speaking their own language to command, and that they be put in a position to do their best and work up, if possible, the organization that will be a credit to the province and what they will be proud of. Understanding their mentality as you do, you know that it is far better to appeal to them than force them. They are law abiding and can fight if they wish, as the record of the 22nd shows. Do not hesitate to give them a full chance. We are all watching down here and will be glad to do anything to help the Govern-1221
ment and yourself in this matter, if we are' needed.
Your sincerely,
M. Scarth Stevenson. P.R. DuTremblay, Esq., M.P.,
House of Commons,
Ottawa, Ont.
