It is so obviously fair that the course which I have suggested be adopted, that hon. gentlemen will, perhaps, wonder why some action has not already been taken in the matter. One of the arguments made by the Prime Minister the other day was that we had not the material necessary to the formation of a French Canadian brigade.
I shall not discuss the reasons why a French Canadian brigade was not formed, but I wish to point out that under the compulsory service law the men can easily be found, and one Teason against it therefore disappears. How can the formation of a French Canadian brigade best be accomplished? Two suggestions have been made, one of which, I think, was considered the better by the Prime Minister in the interview which 1 had with him some weeks ago. On the battle line in France there are. seven regiments from Quebec, one, the 22nd, composed entirely of French Canadians, and the other six commanded by British officers, each containing 200, 300 or 400 French Canadians. One way of forming the French Canadian brigade would be by furnishing reinforcements of French Canadians as these are needed. In this way, the units would soon become composed of French Canadians. The Minister of Militia and the Prime Minister are, I know, disposed to favour the grouping of French Canadians, but difficulty is met with in England because the military authorities there do not want to send raw recruits to the front; they want to send seasoned men.

What does the hon. gentleman mean by speaking of meeting difficulties in England? Who present the ' difficulties, the British Government or the Canadian Government, in England?
Mr. DuTREMBLAY: The hon. gentleman might better direct his question to his own side of the House, and seek a reply from the Prime Minister or the Minister of Militia. However, it is true that it may not be desirable to send to the front as a complete unit men who have never been under fire.

What I want to make clear is whether the British Government is the origin of the difficulties to which my hon. friend refers. If there is any opposition, it is not from the British Govern-

ment. I do not want the British Government branded as interfering in Canadian affairs.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Sir Sam Hughes) is quite right. There *was no suggestion from the British Government on the subject.

I should think not.
Mr. DuTREMBiLAY:	I understand that
these regiments must be composed of men who are prepared to fight in the battle line, and the difficulty would be in changing the officers. But officers competent to command French Canadian regiments may easily be found in large numbers. These seven regiments from Quebec could easily be constituted entirely of French Canadians, because under the present military service law four-fifths of the recruits from Quebec speak the French Canadian language. It is well, therefore, that the military authorities should decide this question at once and take the necessary steps to ensure that these regiments shall be reinforced by French Canadians and that men speaking the French Canadian language shall be in command of them.
A few suggestions were made to me by a French Canadian officer of high standing who went to the front and was wounded, regarding the formation of a French Canadian brigade. He suggested:
1.	The initial step to toe taken is to appoint a director of personnel .and personal services in Canada and in England. This position is of great importance and must be Ailed by an officer of high rank and one who has full knowledge of past methods of dealing with these matters and intimate knowledge of present conditions in Canada. He must be given the rank of brigadier-general in order to afford him the necessary prestige and protection it is an absolute necessity that he have a good record. Lieutenant-Colonel La FlSche, D.S.O. Chevalier of the Legion of Honour, is one of the few suitable to fill this mission. Owing to his wounds he is not fit for duty at the front, and being decorated by both the English and the French Governments, makes an ideal liason between the two races. Special duty: to look after French Canadian man-power in Canada.
2.	Brigade organization. Complement: officers 140, men 4,000.
He suggested that the command of that brigade be given to Lieutenant-Colonel Tremblay, D.S.O., officer of the Legion of Honour, who should be given the rank of brigadier-general. As hon. gentlemen are aware, Colonel Tremblay is the hero who to-day commands the glorious 22nd in France. He has already had the experience of commanding a brigade in France on different occasions, though he has not had the 
rank or the pay of a brigadier-general. It is evident that Colonel Tremblay would be well competent to fulfil the duties suggested. The officer further says:
Colonel Tremblay has commanded the famous 2.2nd Battalion for over two years, is known as one of the very best and bravest officers in France, and has on several occasions commanded the brigade. This officer is loved toy all who have fought under him and who have known him. He, of course, should have full power to choose his own officers. The names of the following officers are given to prove that there are easily enough senior officers to supply a brigade:	(Major A. E. Dutouc, D.SXX,
Chevalier of the Legion of Honour; Lieutenant-Colonel H. Barre, Chevalier of the Legion of Honour; Lieutenant-Colonel Desrosiers, Lieut-tenant-Colonel L. R. LaFlSche, D.S.O., Chevalier of the Legion of Honour; Major Vanier, M.C., Chevalier of the Legion of Honour; Major Henri Chassfi, M.C.; Lieutenant-Colonel Piuze. Major R. L. Calder; Major DeSerres ; Major L. Gauvreau ; Major J. P. U. Arch'ambault, Lieutenant-Colonel Dansereau; Captain Leo M. Duval, (M.C.; (Major Asselin; Lieutenant-Colonel Verret, D.S.O.; Lieutenant-Colonel Lefebvre.
There are at present enough officers with experience at the front to fill the positions of company commanders and platoon commanders. Most of the officers are in France or England, though several are now in Canada. To meet the wastage amongst junior officers, a school of officers should (be organized in Canada.
We should have a French Canadian officers' training corps in the province of Quebec. I make the charge against the Government that if it wanted to have a fall measure of enlistment from amongst the French Canadians in the province of Quebec, it should have established, since the beginning of the war, a school for officers in that province. The officer goes on. The letter continues:
Applicants to toe very oarefully chosen. They should he tried1 out in Canada, and when proven to be likely subjects to be sent to England, to complete their course where they would he ready to proceed to France to fill vacancies. This measure is most important, as many young men have not enlisted, and knowing that under present conditions they must go as privates, they are not satisfied. By overcoming this difficulty, a remarkable change will be felt regarding the Military Service Act, and while cultivating the very necessary esprit de corps, these men will bring popularity to the brigade, thereby creating a needed strength and sympathy for our fighting army and its members.
One thousand men, seasoned warriors now fighting in France (22n<3 Battalion) to he withdrawn and divided into four groups of 250 men. To each group 750 trained men who have not been under fire are to be added to form a battalion. Given that a. sufficient number of trained men are now available in England, or If not, they should shortly toe (draftees recently sent over), this organization should take between six to eight weeks. Recruiting under the present arrangements fully provides for

wastage as French Canadian draftees are now expected to keep up over four English-speaking Quebec province Battalions, now at the front. All officers and men destined for this -brigade should be recruited and .trained in French-Canadian units, viz., Depot Battalions in Canada, and training battalions in England. This for maintenance of esprit de corps, development of self-confidence, pride of race and standardization of training.
As I have said, had this request been acceded to by this Government, certain misunderstandings in the province of Quebec would have been cleared away, because I am informed that French Canadian officers at the front would rather serve with their own people. The methods by which this end is to be obtained cannot be roundabout; they must be direct and to the point, and the Government should announce to the public that it is their intention to form a French Canadian brigade so that confidence may be restored to the people of the province of Quebec, and the Prime Minister knows well that confidence in the people begets confidence in the Government.
There is a special reason why a French Canadian brigade should be authorized in the province of Quebec, and that is the reason of language. The same reason does not apply in other provinces where there is unity of language. The Prime Minister seems to have good intentions in regard to this matter. If the Prime Minister will put aside criminal appeals from fanatics and follow his own good inclinations; if he will put himself on a high level of patriotism, then he will go dow.n in history with the other great prime ministers as having been able to rise above petty questions of party and politics when a question of national unity and justice to the minority is at stake. I conclude with this appeal, that on this question the hon. members of this" House will be true to themselves, aye, and above all, true to those brave boys who are fighting.for us in France and Flanders, for our liberty and our future happiness.
tSir ROBERT BORDEN: My hon. friend (Mr. DuTremblay) has spoken very earnestly on this subject, and I can assure him that, so far as his object can be carried out in conformity with military exigencies at the front, there is every disposition on the part of the Government to aid in every way. I am not altogether sure, and I think my hon. 'friend would not be altogether sure, that the mixing of men from other provinces with men from the province of Quebec in one company or one battalion would he without advantage. The difficulty
in the past has been that men from different provinces have not been associated so as to know each other, to understand each other, to realize each other's viewpoint, and the good qualities of each other. That lack of understanding could perhaps, be obviated in the most effective way by putting men from different parts of the country side by side in the same company or the same battalion to fight for the same common cause. But I realize the force of the considerations to which my hon. friend has directed attention. We are not in the least unmindful of them, and we realize further the splendid courage and the fine achievements of French Canadians at the front, notably the 22nd Regiment. I speak particularly of that regiment at Ooureellette, because, when Courcellette was captured, side by side with the 22nd Regiment fought a regiment from my own province. It unfortunately has been necessary to break up a good many units that have gone overseas, when it seemed almost cruel to do so. The Minister of Militia and Defence informs me that the city of Hamilton, from which he comes, has raised 10,000 men, and it is not represented at the front at present by a single distinctive unit.

Nineteen is the number of the Hamilton Battalion. It is still in harness.
Major-General MEWBTTRN: Only a company and a half.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
We have had the same experience in Nova Scotia. The Nova Scotians raised a very fine body of men called the Nova Scotia Highland Brigade. They went across the seas as a brigade, but it was necessary when they got overseas to break the brigade up. One regiment went to the front, another joined the 5th division and two others were used as depot regiments.
I would like to say that the idea of raising a brigade of Canadians of French descent is not by any means new, and I would like my hon. friend to know this, and perhaps my hon. friend' the ex-Minister of Militia and Defence (Sir Sam Hughes) can tell him something further; I remember that in June, 1916, I had a personal interview with General Lessard and asked him to undertake the raising of a brigade of French Canadians, and to take command of it and lead it to the front. He found himself unable to undertake the task at that time and it has never been under-

taken since. My horn, triend (Mr. Du Tremblay) has alluded' to a conversation which he had with me on the subject, in which I expressed, as I felt then and feel now, a great deal of sympathy with the purpose that he has in view. If French Canadians would like to have a greater number of distinctive regiments, and a French Canadian brigade, then so far as. military exigencies will permit we ought to do everything possible to facilitate their formation. But my hon. friend will realize that it would be .most unwise for the Government of this country to impose upon the military authorities at the front an undertaking which in the judgment of those authorities might be productive of disaster. It might be not only unfair, but positively cruel to send into the trenches a .brigade of troops with only such training as they could get in camp, and without that acquaintance with the methods of trench warfare which is all essential. I was told in France a year ago last month that some of the methods of warfare in vogue a year before that had been absolutely discontinued. New conditions are developing all the time and new needs have to be met. Men have to be trained to the utmost limit before they are put into the trenches. I think, although I speak with no great knowledge of the subject, the usual practice is to put a portion of a new battalion in with men who have had experience in the trenches, in order that the new men may learn from their more experienced comrades how best to. perform their duty and to meet the enemy.
But. there is a possibility that something along the line of what my hon. friend suggests might be accomplished through the methods to which he alluded, or through some method analagous to that. I sent a telegram to the Overseas Minister, who communicated with Sir Arthur Currie with regard to it, and. I received a reply giving expression to what Sir Arthur Currie thought might be done. The suggestion, in part at least, was this: that reinforcements for battalions and .regiments at the front which at the present time contain a considerable number of French Canadians might Ibe provided out of men of French descent who are now going forward from the province of Quebec, and in that way, by a gradual process such as. my hon. friend has described, regiment after regiment now containing a certain proportion of French Canadians might be so supplied with reinforcements that eventually they would attain a distinctive character as French Canadian units, 
and in that way very probably a brigade might be formed. I do not know whether it would be practicable to form it in any other way. My hon. friend, who was good enough to communicate to me .privately his own views which he has- expressed on the floor of the House to-day, will realize, I hope, that I have the utmost sympathy with the purpose he has in mind, but he wild also realize, I trust, that in respect of all these m/atters the Government must naturally take into account the judgment of the military authorities, at the front, who are much more capable of judging what is possible and what is not possible in these matters than I or than any other member of this House could possibly be. So I leave the matter at that for the moment, subject to what my colleague the Minister of Militia and Defence (Major-General Mewburn) may say with regard to it. I emphasize once more my desire, so far as military exigencies will permit, to assist in the purpose which uny hon. friend has at heart.
May we hope to have a further communication from the Government on this subject before the end of the session?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I have given really about all the information that has, up to the present time, come from Sir Arthur Currie, but if there is anything that I can usefully add before the end of the session I can assure my right hon. friend that I shall be only too glad to communicate it to the House. I shall use any further endeavours of which I am capable to assist in accomplishing this purpO.se.

I would respectfully dissent from the suggestion that the arrangement of these matters should be left to the Canadian command at the front. That practice should never have been followed in the first place, and should not be followed now. I know of one Canadian battalion which in three months after Lens wasted upwards of four thousand men. The 50th Battalion of Calgary in one year lost' nine thousand men and one hundred and eighteen officers. The gentleman who so informed me is in the gallery to-day and was one of the unfortunates who were bowled out. It is this kind of generalship that has prevented not only the formation long ago of French Canadian brigades, but of a sixth division and two army corps ip the field. In the summer of 1916 we had a plan for six division, two army corps, and a French Canadian brigade. The whole thing was thoroughly planned, One battalion was

from the Eastern Townships; I forget the commander's name, but he was a cavalry officer, an Englishman; I think it was Colonel Gilbert. Nearly half of that battalion were French,- and they were perfectly satisfied to come ini with the other three French Canadian battalions. We were going to organize them into a brigade, but the whole .plan was knocked on the head. It was not necessary, of course, to break up these battalions. The Nova Scotian Highlanders, one of the finest brigades that ever wore uniform, were broken up after the solemn pledge of the Prime Minister that they would go forward as a unit. It was. some officer or power in England-
I know what it is but I will not discuss it -that was responsible for the breaking up of this brigade, just as it was responsible for preventing the formation of a sixth division and two army corps, instead of one army corps and four divisions. Our losses with two army corps would not have been any heavier. Take the case of the Calgary battalion that I mentioned a moment ago. It lost nine thousand men in twelve months and was filled up, filled up, filled up, and filled up again in the twelve months. What difference would it have made if those nine thousand casualties had been spread over three battalions instead of , one? I maintain that if my plan had been followed we would have had at the front to-day six divisions and two army corps, and then we would have avoided the troubles the Prime Minister will find among those men when he gets over there this summer. We would also have had a French Canadian brigade commanded by a French Canadian officer. There are scores of gallant French Canadian officers, without dragging in General Lessard, who have covered themselves with glory and were not afraid to face the music. We could have had all this in 1916 if the plans I laid down had been followed.
The right hon. the Prime Minister referred to the new Conditions of warfare. General Rawlinson, with one man to a yard and a half, held back 25 Germans to the yard, trimmed them to a finish and held the trenches. He defeated the Germans 25 men to a yard and did not seem to have much trouble in doing it, and there was not a man between Rawlinson and Calais. These men were armed with Lee-Enfield rifles. The Canadian corps at St. Julien and at the second battle of Ypres with practically a similar number of hien, one Canadian to every two yards, held back from 12 to 25 Germans to the yard.
It chanced that the Canadians were armed with Ross rifles on Ithat occasion. I am sorry to say that the conditions of warfare are very much changed since that time, that rifle shooting seems to have fallen back, and that bombs, hand grenades, and ail those side shows have taken its place, with results that are not altogether too satisfactory, as is shown by the loss of Cambrai and St. Quentin, where we did not cover ourselves with too much glory. There is one thing more and that is that if you train the men to feel their own power there is no power in Germany that can drive them back.
Major-General MEWBURN (Minister of Militia and Defence): Mr. Speaker, I regret that I was unable to be present when my hon. friend (Mr. DuTremblay) spoke, but I should like to say one or two words because he was good enough to speak to me yesterday regarding his suggestion as to forming a French Canadian brigade. It would be very easy for me to get into a critical mood and go back to the early stages of the war and find fault with the organization of our Canadian forces. It would be an easy matter for some to play the old game of criticising my good friend the former Minister of Militia and Defence (Sir Sam Hughes). But I must say that he is entitled to every credit for doing the utmost that any human being could do, and for the wonderful effort he made in raising the first and second contingents. I always objected to. the methods by which he did it, and I do not hesitate to say so here. I have no hesitation in saying that, if he had allowed the old .militia units, which had been in existence for many years to have gone over, and held their original designations, and to raise one, two, or three battalions within themselves for reinforcements, it probably would have been better all round. We might have got better results if that policy had been adopted, but I shall not go into that now. I am trying to view the situation as it stands .to-day.
Sir .SAM HUGHES:	Would my hon.
friend have had each battalion of the old militia force represented at the front as a corps? If so, he would have had about 200 battalions.
Major-General MEWBURN:	We have at
the front today in the four divisions 48 infantry battalions, not including the pioneer battalions and line of communication troops. We had in Canada autogether about

120 infantry battalions including the rural corps. I believe it would have been a very-simple matter to have allowed a certain number of city battalions, and also some rural battalions which could have been made into composite battalions, t.o have been trained and to have gone to the front under their own regimental numbers, allowing these units to have raised as many battalions within themselves as they could. Those were my views and the views of some other members of the militia at that time. In the fall of 1915 a good many of us asked the. then Minister of Militia and Defence if he would permit us in Military District No. 2 to raise an Ontario division for the front. He agreed and promised a division from Ontario. It was raised and organized in all its component parts, except the Howitzer brigade, but the military situation -was such that it did not work out as we had hoped it would, and we were told it was not possible to carry out the scheme as we had supposed. We still "carried on," did a lot of work, got men, and we did achieve very good results.
It is not within my power to-day to say that a French Canadian brigade may be raised from the province of Quebec; that it shall go overseas as a bridagde; and that we shall take out one of the brigades at present at the front and substitute for it a new brigade. But I think my hon. friend will agree that I have gone out of my way [DOT]-and it has been a pleasure to me to do it -to meet in every way possible the views of my hon. friends who have shown such a magnificent desire to get men from the province of Quebec. I have done everything in my power to meet that situation, i realize the fact that not only in their interest, but in the interest of the service, it is most desirable that men coming from the same localities and men of the same condition in life should be kept together, and have opportunity of associating together both in training and at the front.
Let me refer to the formation of the first Tank battalion that has been raised in Canada. W|e received instructions from overseas to raise a tank battalion. We thought it well to immediately get in touch with the various universities in Canada, we communicated with them, and the result is that we have in the city of Ottawa to-day the first Tank battalion raised in Canada.

How many men?
Major-General MEWBURN:	Nearly 800
men. It will be the privilege of the members of this House to see that Tank batta-[Major Genera] Mewburn.]
lion on parade in front of the Parliament Buildings on Friday afternoon before- they leave for overseas. That is the first battalion of that kind that has been raised in Canada and it is most creditable to my friends from the province of Quebec that they rose to the occasion and raised their quota for that corps. The result has been so gratifying that the question has been asked me by some members, " Could we not attempt a second Tank battalion." I did not hesitate to say that I thought we could, and I have already cabled overseas to see if -we can get permission to raise a second Tank battalion in- Canada.
As to a French Canadian brigade, I may say we have been in communication with the universities in the province of Quebec, and I am glad to say that Laval University both in Montreal and in Quebec has met us in a splendid spirit, and has undertaken to raise two companies from the C.O. T.C. I shall do all in my power not only to secure further reinforcements for our troops but to promote that solid unity of sentiment that should exist between the people of the different provinces of Canada.
That is my fond hope and desire and just as soon as I can get away from Parliament I shall take a trip through the province of Quebec to see what further can be done to put that plan into effect. I hope and sincerely trust that the C.O.T.C. to which I have referred, will not be the only one in the province of Quebec. As to whether a French Canadian brigade can be authorized and raised, or as to whether -a French Canadian brigade can be sent to the front, it is not for me to say. That must be left to the Commander of the Force in France.

May I remind the House that a communication was made to us this morning from the convention of farmers now in session in Ottawa? These farmers have asked us to give them an appointment so that two or three representatives from their conference might address this House. I have been advised by one of the members from Ontario of -the executive committee, that they will be in session at the Arena from two o'clock until six this afternoon and that their executive is expecting the answer that was promised by your letter, Mr. Speaker, in reply to their communication of this morning.
I venture to suggest that it may be proper to determine, first, whether we are going to receive these farmers, then fix the hour

for doing so; and then inform them of cur decision without delay so that they could make arrangements to meet us at the appointed time.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I rise to speak with the permission of the House, because I have spoken already. I had the privilege this morning, for two hours and a half, of attending a meeting with the delegates to whom my hon. friend has made allusion, and it does not seem to me desirable at this stage of the session that the proceedings of the House should be interrupted for the purpose' which he has mentioned.

Hear, hear.
iSir ROBERT BORDEN: I am in a position whenever the House so desires to make it acquainted with the views which were expressed at that meeting, and under the circumstances I do not feel that the House ought to interrupt its proceedings for the purpose referred to. If these gentlemen would like, between the hours of six and eight o'clock, to address any members of the House who would wish to be present to hear them, there is not the slightest objection to it, but to interrupt for that purpose, the proceedings during the ordinary hours at which this House meets, seems out of the question under present conditions.

subsubtopic: PURCHASE OF HAND FOR THE CAMP SITE.
speechtext:
Before you leave the Chair, Mr. Speaker, I wish to draw the attention of the Minister of Militia and Defence to the manner in tvhich the expropriation of land for Camp Borden was carried, out. A motion in my name in regard to this matter has been on the Order Paper from the beginning of the session until lately, when, as it could not be reached, owing to the advanced state of the session, by agreement with the right hon. leader of the House, I allowed it to be dropped with the understanding that I should be free to bring the subject up on going into Supply. My remarks on this occasion will be short and to the point.
The matter in itself is of some importance. Prior to the war, Mr. Speaker, the military authorities in Canada had secured
359,000	acres of military camp ground. After the war my hon. friend the Minister of Militia and Defence, acquired for the Government, and. rightly so, the now famous Valcartier camp, which brought the total acreage of military camp grounds to
372,000	acres. Later on, in May of the year 1916, the Government further acquired what is now known as Camp Borden in the province of Ontario, comprising in the neighbourhood of 16,200 acres. In addition, Mr. Speaker, the Militia Department controls other areas of land known as the Dorval property, the old La Prairie camp, and the Rockcliffe and Connaught rifle ranges. The contract between the Minister of Militia and Defence and the would-be owner or proprietor of the property which has since become well known as the Borden camp, was made on the 10th April, 1916. The contract was entered into between the Hon. Edward Kemp, now Sir Edward Kemp -who was then the Acting Minister of Militia and Defence,-and a gentleman by the name of James Barr.

subsubtopic: PURCHASE OF HAND FOR THE CAMP SITE.
speechtext: I might point out [DOT]that it was not the Minister of Militia and Defence, it was the acting minister who entered into that contract.

subsubtopic: PURCHASE OF HAND FOR THE CAMP SITE.
speechtext:
I am glad to be corrected by my hon. friend.. It was the Acting Minister of Militia and Defence. The contract was for the delivery of 17,300 acres of land for the sum of $207,600, at the rate of $12 per acre. James Barr obtained the land. He was the owner of a certain portion, but obtained the balance from divers owners at the rate of $8 per acre, and in some cases even less. Barr represented himself as the Government agent, and offered to many of the parties, as I will show in a moment, from $3 to $8 per acre for the land which he sought to acquire, he. himself having an agreement at that time with the then Acting Minister of Militia and Defence under which he was to receive $12 an acre. At first the owners resisted and protested when asked to dispose of their property. Some of them had enlisted and gone overseas, and the bargain wrns made with their wives or relatives. As there was on their part a fear of the law and of long drawn-out litigation and proceedings before the Exchequer Court, with consequent delays and appeals to the courts, most, if not all, of the owners, agreed to accept the amounts which were offered to them.
Now in order to make this case very clear and to show how those poor people were duped, I will first of all read the agreeement entered into between the Acting Minister of Militia and Defence and James Barr. I need not describe the lands themselves, which are well known in char-

subsubtopic: PURCHASE OF HAND FOR THE CAMP SITE.
speechtext: Who signs that as witness?

subsubtopic: PURCHASE OF HAND FOR THE CAMP SITE.
speechtext: The witness is F. B. Poucher, evidently an old French name.

subsubtopic: PURCHASE OF HAND FOR THE CAMP SITE.
speechtext: Is he the land valuator of the National Trust Company?

subsubtopic: PURCHASE OF HAND FOR THE CAMP SITE.
speechtext:
I have seen his name connected with the National Trust, but as to that I cannot vouch. Mr. Poucher could vouch, I suppose. Now, Mr. Barr evidently had in mind to get the balance of the property at as cheap .a price as possible. He was already in possession of 8,000 acres. He retained the services of a gentleman named G. A. Radenhurst, solicitor, barrister, notary public and conveyancer, of Barrie, Ont. I will give the letter which this barrister wrote to the various parties owning the balance of the lots:
Barrie, November 25, 1916. Dear Sir,-	[DOT]
I enclose you herewith the formal tender on behalf of the Crown-
You -see, he represents himself as acting for the Crown, that is, for the Department oif Militia and Defence.
-for the lands expropriated as part of Camp Borden. I would be glad if you would let me know whether it is accepted or not, and if not accepted the name of any solicitor who would accept service for you of the Information to be lodged. Also if the lot named in the tender is not the property you are interested in, or if you are interested in any other property in the said site not settled for, please let me know. The Crown is only anxious-
Always speaking on behalf of the Crown, for the Department of Militia and Defence.
[iMr. Lemiieux.l
and in the name of the Acting Minister of Militia and Defence.
-that what is fair and just shall be done, but as the purchasing agent and you differ as to values this is the only course we see that can be fairly taken to ascertain the value of the lands.
Yours truly,
G. A. Radenhurst.
Many of the unfortunate proprietors, fearing long-drawn out expropriation proceedings' before the courts, yielded to the demand made by this would-be counsel for the Crown, and it was only after they had received the pittance presumably offered them by the Crown through Mr. Radenhurst, who, in fact, was acting only for James Barr, that they addressed a petition to His Royal Highness the Duke of Connaught, then Governor General. ' I have that petition here, * and shall put it on Hansard:	.
Mimico, Ont., September 26, 1916. To His Royal Highness The Duke of Connaught, Governor General of Canada.
May it please your Royal Highness:
My husband, John Jepson, is a private in the 124th Battalion now in England, and my eldest son is at Camp Borden, and I am living here with my younger children. Four years ago we bought twenty acres which is part of the land taken for Camp Borden. We were well satisfied with the land and intended making our home there, paying for it by hard savings. We have already paid $333, and owe about $25 yet before we get our deed. A man saying he is the purchasing agent for the Government tells us that the Government has taken it and won't pay more than $160. This is a cruel injustice that the Government should rob us of $200, when the only wage-earners of the family are fighting for Canada.
X humbly petition your Royal Highness to [DOT]save my family from this shameful robbery. My husband cannot attend to this himself and I do not know what to do ; so I take this liberty which I hope you will pardon.
Your obedient servant,
Ada Jepson.
Simon Street,
Mimico, Ont.	[DOT]
The secretary of His Royal Highness acknowledged receipt of that letter, and said that it had been referred to the minister-the acting minister I suppose-who would see that justice was done. Mrs. Jepson, however, was nevertheless awarded $160, while James Barr, under his contract with the Acting Minister of Militia and Defence, got $80 profit out of it.

subsubtopic: PURCHASE OF HAND FOR THE CAMP SITE.
speechtext: The hon. member says that this lady was awarded a certain amount. Who awarded it?

subsubtopic: PURCHASE OF HAND FOR THE CAMP SITE.
speechtext:
The Exchequer Court. Mr. Radenhurst got a deed signed by this ladv in the absence of her husband, who

was lighting in France for Canada, and fearing that it would come before the courts, and being under the impression that Raden-hurst and Barr were acting for the Crown, she yielded.
Let us take the case of William Russell, . No. 29 Rusholme Park Crescent, Toronto, County of York, also on the matter of Camp Borden. I have here his affidavit. He was the owner of twenty acres, Mr. Speaker, in that site taken for the Government for Camp Borden. He had paid $17 per acre for it, had bought it after personal inspection for his summer home, and was well satisfied with it. What took place in his case? He will recite the facts:
That in order to get me to sell for less than it cost, a man named James Barr claiming to be the Government agent offered me $8 per acre, stating that was all the Government would pay, and if I did not take that price it would be confiscated by the Government. Previous to that, he offered my wife $3 per acre, using the same threats to her and stating that he had got lots of the land at that price, which I quite believe if he used the same means to acquire it, especially when his conduct was endorsed by Radenhurst, the Government solicitor, who referred to Barr as the purchasing agent and repeated his offer at $8, stating that the Crown is only anxious that what is fair and just should be done, but as the purchasing agent (Barr) and you differ as to values, etc. I have since ascertained that at the time Barr tried to compel my wife to sell for $3 he had already sold my land to the Government for $12 per acre.
So there was a clear gain of $4 per acre inuring to James Barr. Russell continues:
My son bought the adjoining lot at the same time. He is now fighting with the Canadian army in France and he is treaied in the same way as I am. We each are offered less than half our cost and have both costs to pay, while Barr's costs are paid by the Government. I have two sons in the fighting line including the one they are trying to rob.
(Signed) W. Russell.
Then there is another case in which the Government paid $160, by the same device, for land which had cost the owner $670, J-ames Barr making quite a profit on the deal. A man by the name of George Behe, of Toronto, solemnly declares:
I am nearly sixty years of age, working in a factory for my daily bread, and bought this land by hard savings, to live oq when too old for factory work. I am well satisfied with the land, and diq not wish to sell it. I have sent three sons to the war; my eldest, George, was killed at Ypres ; my second, Harry, was wounded four times, twice whilq acting as doctor's assistant and continued dressing the wounded after the doctor was killed, for which he received the D.S. Medal, and I have to-day received# a telegram that my third son; Tom, of the 204th regiment is severely wounded. I am told that the Canadian Government have taken my land without my consent and offered me
$160 for it. Canada, not content with my giving three sons to her defence, proposes now to rob me of $520.
(Signed) J. G. Behe.

subsubtopic: PURCHASE OF HAND FOR THE CAMP SITE.
speechtext: What are the numbers of the lots and concessions in the cases referred to?

subsubtopic: PURCHASE OF HAND FOR THE CAMP SITE.
speechtext:
This man Behe said that in November, 1911, he bought twenty acres in lot 28, fifth concession, Tossorontio, paying for the said lot $320. He says that wire fencing, clearing and putting under cultivation cost him $350, a total of $670. In the other oases the numbers and descriptions of the lots are not given, but my hon. friend may obtain the official numbers from the department. My object in moving for the papers in this case was to get the titles and papers generally from the Exchequer Court proceedings.
In another case the property of a soldier at the front was sacrificed to make a profit of $80 for this man James Barr. The affidavit in this case is given by a lady, Isabel Tubb, who solemnly declares:
Henry Herbert Tubb was the owner of twenty acres included in the site taken by the Government for Camp Borden, which cost him $16 per acre. That in order to get him to sell It for less than it cost, a man claiming to be the Government agent wrote to me from Barrie and offered $8 per acre and stated that was the highest amount the Government would pay. The said party making the offer was the Crown Solicitor acting for the Government in the matter. The said Henry Herbert Tubb is now overseas and all business has been transacted through me, his wife.
That is, through herself. She declares that she has full knowledge of the matters in question.
Another case was that of George Buxton, who was the owner of 20 acres, being part of lot 27 in the fifth concession included in the site taken by the Government for Camp Borden. It had cost George Buxton $350 and for it he was offered by James Barr and a man named C. F. Wright, both claiming to be Government agents, $8 per acre. Both said that the amount offered was all the Government could pay and that unless George Buxton would take that price he might have to fight the Government for three years and finally get nothing. According to Buxton's affidavit, both these men, Wright and Barr, stated explicitly that they were employed by tne Government and that the Government would not give more than $8 per acre. Of course Barr was pocketing the difference between $8 and $12 per acre
Another case was that of I. F. Berry, of
Toronto, who solemnly declares:

On the 16th August 1911 I went up to Lisle with a friend and selected the forty acres after full inquiry and personal inspection. My friend bought forty acres at the same time. We tested the land and considered it worth a great deal more than the $15 we paid for it. It was better than the advertisement said as we found qualities which had not been mentioned. We went up alone and paid our own expenses. On February 1, 1916, I paid my last instalment after much saving and self-denial, intending shortly to go on the land. The forty acres has cost me altogether $700 and represents all my savings for six years, But my land had a special value. It was near the river and in developing the water power my land would be absolutely necessary. Mr. Radenhurst, the Government's solicitor, -wrote me that the Government would not take my land without just and fair compensation and advised me to see Wright and Barr, College Street. Wright and Barr sent a man named Barnes to see me and said Wright and Barr had been appointed by the Government to buy the land and -would give me $8 per acre and if I refused I would have to fight the Government and that such cases lasted for years.
He also said- the Government was getting land for less and would not in any case pay over $8. I have since learned that Mr. Barr had already sold my land to the Government for $12, expecting to compel me by threats to sell for $8, so he could make $160 at my expense. Mr. Radenhurst helped him all he could to compel me to sell my land at a loss of $450. The Government should at least give me what I paid for the land1 and order Barnes, Wright and Barr to be arrested, if the sentiments of right and justice have any influence. The land is assessed for $400, and I have paid taxes on that valuation.
The mulcted third parties have, through His Excellency the Governor General in Council, petitioned the present Government, and I sincerely hope the Government *will live up to that sense of fair play and justice which must animate every true Britisher and Canadian. Here are men whose sons are at the front, some of them having been wounded; here are men who have given as many as three sons to the cause of liberty and justice; here are women whose only support is a husband or a son at the front, and during the absence of those dear ones, speculators have the audacity to represent themselves as being Government agents and Crown solicitors, and 'by their representations they get signatures from those unsuspicious, honest people, because the latter fear that if they plead with the Government before the courts of the land, their cases will take many years to decide and thus they sacrifice the earnings and the properties which they have acquired after many years of hard and unremitting toil.
I hope the sense of British fair play which ought to animate the Government in the present instance will exhibit itself, and that, after investigation, those people will
[Mr. Lemieux.i
be reimbursed the moneys that have been snatched away from them by those agents. I do not accuse; I make no charge against the Department of Militia and Defence; I make qo charge against the Government; but I say that, now that I have made public the facts and that they are known officially, it is the Sbounden duty of the Government to hold an inquiry into those matters and to see that justice is done.
This is the petition which has been forwarded to His Excellency the Governor General in Council by the aggrieved parties:
Whereas, by a certain -agreement entered into between the Hon, A. E. Kemp, Acting Minister of Militia for the Dominion of Canada, and James Barr, of the city of Toronto, province of Ontario, dated April 14, 1916, the Government of the Dominion of Canada undertook to purchase -at $12 an- acre some 17,300 acres described in the aforementioned agreement as situate, lying and being in the county of Simooe and known popularly as Camp Borden.
And Whereas, after entering into this agreement, the aforementioned James Barr, as the representative of the Minister of Militia, acquired possession of much of this land at $8, and less, .an acre from soldiers in the Canadian Expeditionary Force, their wives and widows, and farmers in none too opulent circumstances ; and- whereas, by the sale to the Government of this land at $12 an acre in pursuance of the aforementioned agreement between Hon. A. E. Kemp and James Barr, the said Barr realized an enormous, and altogether unjustifiable profit.
And Whereas, in the Exchequer Court of Canada, at a session in Toronto on May 17 and 18, 1917, the price paid by the said Barr to the original owners was ratified at expropriation proceedings, the learned trial judge holding .that what Barr had obtained from the Government for the land had nothing to do with the value of the land and the price he paid for it:-
Now therefore, -the following petitioners hum-bly pray that His Majesty's Government may in a spirit _of justice deem it meet and right to order a" further and more thorough inquiry into the transaction in all its ramifications with a view to determining what may be done further towards an equitable adjustment and award.
And your petitioners, as in duty bound, will ever pray.
Though I make no charge against the (Government, I wish however to qualify my statement by saying this, that the Government should never employ go-betweens as between the Crown and the party whose property is to be expropriated. An agreement was made in this case between the Acting MJinister o-f Militia and Defence and Barr by which -a certain piece of property was to be bought by the Government for $12 an acre. Why should the Crown have made such a bargain with James Barr, when the Crown knew perfectly well that Barr was

the owner of only 8,000 acres? The Crown knew perfectly well that the balance was the property of individual owners. The Department of Militia and Defence should have seen to it that the transaction * took place directly between the Crown and the individual owners. From past proceedings and past evidence the department knew very well that any go-between would mulct the third parties in that instance. That is the fault I have to find with the Department of Militia and Defence. But cannot something be now done to right this wrong? We, the representatives of the people, are being asked by this Government on this very day to pay enormous sums to Mac-zenzie and Mann, to the Canadian Northern Railway company; we are being asked to be generous with a company which has	already received millions at
the hands of this Parliament. Mackenzie and Mann are presently claiming before a Board of Arbitration in the city of Toronto, one hundred cents on the dollar as the pretended value of stock which has officially been declared valueless by, commissioners appointed under this Government. It was stated in the Senate at the close of the session last year that the Government was ready to pay up to $10,000,000 in satisfying the claims of Mackenzie and Mann. Surely, if this Government can afford to be so generous as, that with an opulent syndicate, it can afford, not to he generous, but to do what is just and right for the unfortunate wives and young men who are being deprived of the ascertained value of their property at Camp Borden. I would appeal to the sense of fair play and justice in the Government. I do not know these individuals, but if any one in my own province had been treated as these British-born-I am ttold they are British born-have been treated, in the province of Ontario I would be grateful to any one who interceded for my compatriots thus mulcted in the province of Quebec. I say it is a crying shame to let these agents get away with the money of the poor lads who .are fighting our battle in France.

subsubtopic: PURCHASE OF HAND FOR THE CAMP SITE.
speechtext:
Owing to the fact that Camp Borden is within the limits of my riding it may be proper that I should offer an observation or two respecting the matter the bon. member for Maison-neuve (Mr. Lemieux) has just raised. I am sorry I did not know this matter was coming up to-day, for I have considerable information that would have been of great assistance to me, to cite, and which I think
would have assisted this House in coming to a proper conclusion in the matter. I have therefore to speak purely from memory, with, perhaps, a reference to one or two matters that have just been placed in my hands by the minister. In the first place, if what my hon. friend says is strictly correct, not a very strong case has been made out. He refers to $80 in one case, and to about the same amount in another. But he entirely overlooks a feature which I think is a complete answer !to what he has said. He has said that Mr. Barr-may I incidentally remark I hold no brief whatever for Mr. Barr, and have nothing whatever to do with him in any shape or form- he says that Mr. Barr stole eighty dollars. He proceeds upon the assumption that when Barr gets twelve dollars under the contract and only gives eight he is enabled thereby to pocket the sum of four dollars on each acre. If that were so, I would admit at once that, while the figures are not large, the ratio of profit would be exorbitant. But my hon. friend cannot have knowledge of the facts, or I do not think he would have taken his seat leaving any such false impression with the House. If Mr. Barr was not .compelled to give more tliam $12 for some of the lands he bought, or did not have to give more than eight in any case, his argument .might be sound. I myself have a personal knowledge, ll think I may say, of every case of a bona fide settler within the limits of Camp Borden. I have not a knowledge of the three or four cases my hon. friend refers to, nor have I a knowledge of perhaps the most important case, that of Enoch Thompson, a speculator in the .city of Toronto, who had a large acreage within the limits of Camp Borden. But 1 think I have a knowledge of every case of a bona fide settler, for nearly all of them spoke to me and complained they were not getting what they thought was right. In one case a settler got $8,500-I may be two or three hundred dollars out because I am speaking from memory-another one got $7,000, another $6,500, and a number of others got all the way from $1,500 to the figures I have mentioned, all of which averaged more than, far more than $12 an acre. The question this House would require to be answered is to find out whether or not Barr was getting that to which he was not entitled reasonably: How much did he get for the total acreage at Gamp Borden and how much did he pay? Figures were given to me-I cannot say whether they are absolutely accurate or not but if [DOT] they are

accurate I venture to say that no member of this House would have taken over the contract Barr had, and gone to the trouble be did for the profit there was in it. We cannot judge by an odd case here and there; we must have the price that was paid in every case, and perhaps the fairest test as to whether or not the Government have been dealing fairly with the owners of Camp Borden is the fact that out of the whole 16,000 acres only eight or ten claims have not been settled satisfactorily to the owners. In three of these cases there was hardship I admit, but no hardship so far as the action oif the Government is concerned. The hardship was that eight or ten or twelve years ago these innocent, and as far as land values are concerned, ignorant people were induced by somebody, I know not whom, to purchase twenty-acre blocks of land. I know what I am talking about, because I have lived within fourteen miles of this very property all my life. It is pure sand, blow sand.
Mr. LB^IilEUX: If, as my hon. friend says, they are ignorant people is not that all the more reason why the Government should protect them against the wiles of speculators?

subsubtopic: PURCHASE OF HAND FOR THE CAMP SITE.
speechtext: When I said ignorant I had reference to their lack of knowledge of land values in that part of Ontario. They may be cultured people in other respects, but they certainly had no knowledge of the value of this land or they would never have bought it. They were induced by speculators to buy this land at $16 or $20 an acre, not by Barr as far as I know'. In expropriating this land does my hon. friend say it was the duty of the Government to accept las the true value the amount paid. In expropriating proceedings it is the actual value, I understand, not figured too closely, it is true, but rather a little on the generous side that should govern-would my hon. friend say that no matter what a man gave for his property that should be the price paid when expropriating it?

subsubtopic: PURCHASE OF HAND FOR THE CAMP SITE.
speechtext: The least the Government could have done would have been to give these- people the price allowed to Mr. Barr. Mr. Barr got more than the property cost these people.

subsubtopic: PURCHASE OF HAND FOR THE CAMP SITE.
speechtext:
My hon friend cannot have appreciated the argument I made, perhaps feebly and inadequately. Mr. Barr had to give a great deal more than $12 for a great deal of the land he bought. If he had to give $12, and never less, for every acre 
he bought, and sometimes as high as $25 and $30 and $40 an acre for land where there were improvements or barns

there were not very many of them it ie true-he would, have been a loser in the transaction and could not possibly have carried it through. Therefore, he had to acquire some of these lands at less than $12 an acre to be in a position to pay -more than $12 for other lands he had to buy. So after all, it comes down to the question, what has Barr made? Unless we know that, we do not know whether this thing is iniquitous or not.
The hon. gentleman says that there were very many cases. There were, all told, fourteen cases. He says that these will take years to dispose of in the exchequer court. Let me tell him that these fourteen eases have all been disposed of long ago. They went before Mr. Justice Cassels in the exchequer court, a judge in whom I am sure my hon. friend has every confidence. If the matter were of sufficient importance, and time would permit, I would go through these cases. In only two out of the whole fourteen were they successful. In many of the cases the demands were considered -so exorbitant and the land so worthless that his lordship even saddled the claimants with costs. He heard evidence and he found the amount tendered was ample. Unless my hon. friend is prepared to contest what hi-s lordship Mr. Justice Cassels has concluded is the proper way to dispose of values in expropriation cases, that is by giving the actual value and not what these people gave through their ignorance, that puts an end to the case. I do not -think he will go so far as to say that what they paid should be the test. In each case my hon. friend has referred to I asked where the lands were. J visited the location and I found that they were at the west side of the camp in the township of Tossorontio.
I found that the land was blow sand. That is also what was found by Mr. Justice Cassels. Since I have been a member of this House I do not believe there has been any purchase put through a department in the service of this country cleaner or fairer than the Camp Borden transaction and it will stand any investigation that my hon. friend may ask for. You will not find any irregularities there. On the other hand, you will find that there are only a few cases- of dissatisfaction and in these cases these unfortunate people ' gave too much for their land. Mr. Justice Cassels held that what they had given for the land was not a fair test of what it was worth. My hon. friend has forgotten to

state that Mr. Barr had to give more than $12 an acre for some of the land. I think it is hardly fair to accuse him of stealing $80, or the difference between $0 and $12 per acre, because he had to give far more than $12 for a very large acreage in the camp.
My hon. friend, I take it unintentionally and without knowledge, has done a great injustice to Mr. Radenhurst in this connection. If my hon. friend knew Mr. Radenhurst he would never have thought of doing such a thing. If he had not referred to the fact that Mr. Radenhurst was the agent of the department and assisted Barr I would not have: thought it necessary to have dragged his name into this case because he is too respectable and well known in the town of Barrie to be brought into a discussion of this kind. But as my hon. friend has referred to Mr. Barr as stealing, and has coupled Mr. Radenhurst's name with the transaction, 1 feel called upon to protest in defence of one of the most respectable solicitors and gentlemen in the county of Simcoe. If my hon. friend will make any inquiry whatever in the town of Barrie, he will find that there is no one in that locality more honourable and more highly respected than Mr. Radenhurst. He is a man of the highest standing at the bar of the county of Simcoe, is President of the Simcoe Law Association apd is as well known for his honesty and integrity as any man in that county. I think, in view of these facts, that my hon. friend will feel disposed t'o withdraw any insinuations he had made in regard to Mr. Radenhurst.. The only way that my hon. friend can introduce him into the matter is by referring to his letter which he read, but I deny that this letter warrants any such insinuations as my hon. friend has made. In his capacity as agent of the Government, he did what was usual with regard to expropriation proceedings and answered enquiries of land owners felling them if they were not satisfied with the tenders made, the true value could be ascertained by expropriation. When I recall the investigations in the Public Accounts Committee, with regard to Valcartier, I am glad to be the representative of South Simcoe, of the conditions surrounding the purchase in which Camp Borden is, and I derive considerable satisfaction from a comparison of the conditions surrounding the purchase of lands for these two camps. I recall that men from the province of Quebec appeared before that committee and asked $35,000 for farms that were assessed for $900. We had nothing of that kind in the county of Simcoe. The bona fide settlers there were reasonable. Some of them, I thought, asked more than they were entitled to, and I told them so. Mr. Barr was in the office and so was his solicitor. I felt they were 'asking too much and I said to Barr: "As far as I am concerned I want this to be clean, to go through without criticism and without scandal. I don't want excessive prices paid. On the other hand, I want you to be fair to these people." The bulk of the settlers on these lands were humble settlers, although there were five or six good farms in one part. I asked him to loosen up a little bit and do the decent thing. I found Barr willing to do that, and he did it, but he did not do it to excess, in the cases my hon. friend referred to where the land was largely sand.

subsubtopic: PURCHASE OF HAND FOR THE CAMP SITE.
speechtext: With reference to this particular case that has been referred to, were these not little blocks of land that had been sold as a summer resort some years before, where people thought they would have nice little orchards and gardens? There were 25 acres of this land.

subsubtopic: PURCHASE OF HAND FOR THE CAMP SITE.
speechtext:
That is absolutely correct.
The man who promoted that scheme must have hadi some faith in it because I found waterpipes laid down across the land, a gasolene engine and a private waterworks system installed. These lands on the west side of the camp were laid out in blocks and evidently he must have felt that something would grow on them but when I was there there were no signs of vegetation at all. Even the grass would not grow. It Was, as Mr. Justice Cassels found, all blow sand. An effort wae made to show that it was a sort of game preserve. The Pine river goes through some of this property and it was claimed that it was a fishing preserve, that mink, deer and wild1 animals of various descriptions were to be found, and that this represented a certain amount of value. Every conceivable method was devised to add value to this property. 1 do not think any .hon. gentleman will say for a moment that Mr. Justice Cassels had any idea of putting a lower value upon this land than the actual value. If my hon. friend will take the time to go through the six or seven typewritten pages of the judgment of Mr. Justice Cassels the ideas which .he has as to the situation at Camp Borden will be very quickly removed with this one exception which I am free a.t all times to admit, and that is that a hardship exists owing solely to the fact that they paid too

much when they bought years ago. If you are to lay down the law that because a man has given $20 per acre for his property, even if it is only worth $3, he should get $20, these men should have received more money. But I do not think my hon. friend can find any such law. Mr. Justice Cassels found to the contrary. There are some other features but I do not feel that it is desirable that I should take up more time at this stage. I want to point out in conclusion, for the benefit of those gentlemen who have not seen Camp Borden, that I do not believe there is any place in 'Canada where the 'Government could have secured 16,000 acres for anything like the same money more suitable for a military camp than the land within	the limits	of	that camp.
And in doing that I am not going by my own judgment. I have talked with officers who have been in the camps of Great Britain, and have been in all the camps in Canada-in Ontario and Quebec, at all events-and they have told me that all things being considered there is not a better camp in England or in Canada. There is, for instance, an abundant supply of the purest water that could be got anywhere. Artesian wells were sunk six inches across -one of them eight inches across-to a depth of 125 feet, thus securing an abundant flow of as fine drinking water as you could possibly get, and that is a most important feature in connection with such a camp. It is true that on one particular day of extreme heat, more than a year ago, there was considerable 'dust, mainly caused by the burning of hundreds and thousands of stumps, but you did not hear that complaint last year, and I do not believe you will hear it again. I only want to say here that I regret that the Minister of Militia and the department are not able to use Camp Borden to a fuller extent than it is going to be used this year. The Plying Corps, with a strength of some four to five thousand men, which is quite a good number, are located there, but there is room enough at the camp to accommodate thirty thousand-in fact, I think, fifty thousand-troops. The camp is well equipped and fitted to receive men at any time for training while this war goes on. I unhesitatingly say that, although there were some persons who suffered by reason of paying more for their land than they should have done, Camp Borden will bear any investigation that may be intituted and it is refreshing to hear of a case where the Department is accused of not paying enough TMr. Boys.]	.
money, generally the accusation is extra-gance.

speakeroldname: Mr. S. W. JACOBS (George Etienne Cartier) :
subsubtopic: PURCHASE OF HAND FOR THE CAMP SITE.
speechtext:
I have some personal knowledge of this matter through the fact that the legal firm with which I am associated represented some of these parties in the Exchequer Court proceedings, over these lands before Mr. Justice Cassels. I do not wish to approach this case from a sentimental aspect at all. It is purely from the legal point of view that I would like to say a word or two.
I would draw the attention of the House to a very extraordinary clause in the agreement between the Crown and Mr. Barr- the agreement which was referred to by my hon. friend from Maisonneuve (Mr. Le-mieux). It is in a letter addressed to the Hon. A. E. Kemp, Acting Minister of Militia and1 Defence, and signed by James Barr on the 10th April, 1916:
If I am unable to procure any portion of the said property so as to convey the same to you on or before the 10th of May, 1916, you are then to exercise expropriation proceedings in regard to the said property.
"You are to exercise expropriation proceedings in regard to the said property." This is an agreement made by Barr with the Crown. The Crown agrees to pay $12 per acre for this land, and Barr, in order to secure himsellf, makes an agreement containing the proviso that if he should not be-able to secure this land the Crown would give him the machinery of the Exchequer Court, which has hitherto always been reserved to itself, and with this machinery Mr. Barr would wrest from these poor English settlers the land, at the price fixed by the Exchequer Court.

subsubtopic: PURCHASE OF HAND FOR THE CAMP SITE.
speechtext:
I 'think my hon. friend is aware that the proceedings in the Exchequer Court would have to be initiated, not by the department at all, but toy the person who believes that his or her land is worth more than i'S offered.
Mr. JACOB'S: These proceedings were instituted by the Crown.

subsubtopic: PURCHASE OF HAND FOR THE CAMP SITE.
speechtext: Oh, no.

subsubtopic: PURCHASE OF HAND FOR THE CAMP SITE.
speechtext: I am surprised my hon. friend would say that, 'because I acted myself in the case for the parties against the Crown, and >Mr. Badenhurst appeared for the Crown.

subsubtopic: PURCHASE OF HAND FOR THE CAMP SITE.
speechtext: After the offer had been refused.

subsubtopic: PURCHASE OF HAND FOR THE CAMP SITE.
speechtext: Certainly.

subsubtopic: PURCHASE OF HAND FOR THE CAMP SITE.
speechtext: I agree with the hon. gentleman, hut not until the party concerned was unwilling to accept- the amount offered-.

subsubtopic: PURCHASE OF HAND FOR THE CAMP SITE.
speechtext: Certainly, but Mr. Barr offerer! $8 per acre to these people and they refused to accept it. He then threatened them with .Exchequer Court proceedings, and when they still remained bbdurate, we find the Crown appearing as- plaintiff in the case, (although they had made arrangements with Barr to purchase that property from him for $12 an acre. They gave him the machinery of the Exchequer Court so that he would obtain the land from these -people at the price fixed by the court. The case came on and the Crown, mark you, that had made arrangements to pay $12 an acre for -the land a few -months before, placed witnesses on the stand to prove that the land for which it had agreed to pay $12 an acre was not worth more than $8 an acre, and the Court so found, and further found- that some of the land was not even worth $3 an acre. It maintained Mr. Barr in his contention. My complaint against the Crown is this : Had it not made this arrangement to give Barr the machinery of the Exchequer Court to obtain this land, Barr would have been in the same position as any other man, and owners could have held their land against the world; they might have asked $10,000 per acre, and Mr. Barr would not have been able to take it from them. But under this agreement the people found they had to part with their land, not to the Crown, but to a private individual, and the quarrel I have with the Crown is that it should have prostituted its position, and handed over the machinery of the Exchequ-qer Court to a private individual, for his own gain, so that these men had to part with their property for $8 when they could have held it for any price they liked. That is- the position.	*

speechtext: I do not know, Mr. Speaker, if I am in order to speak on the matter.

subsubtopic: PURCHASE OF HAND FOR THE CAMP SITE.
speechtext: Yes, the hon. member has already spoken.

speechtext: Not on this question.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: PURCHASE OF HAND FOR THE CAMP SITE.
PURCHASE OF HAND FOR THE CAMP SITE.
speechtext: Is it a fact that Mr. Barr paid in any one instance more than $12 an acre for that land?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: PURCHASE OF HAND FOR THE CAMP SITE.
speechtext:
He owned some
5,800 acres, but what -he paid for it I do- not know. This much I do know; that before the Crown determined' to buy the entire site at that aggregate price it h-ad the land valued by two outstanding valuators of the city of Toronto, whose reputations certainly are above suspicion, who valued the entire area and put upon the land the price that was paid for it, taking one lot with another. We are not undertaking to say that each particular lot w-as worth $12. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Jacobs) asked if Mr. Barr paid more than $12 for any one acre. As I said I do not know what he paid for the land, but I would point out this fact, which establishes beyond peradven-ture that some thousand's of acres of the land included in the original quantity were worth more than $12 an acre; that subsequently to that contract there was a further arrangement entered into in virtue whereof the -Crown could abandon any part of the land- which it found not to be required, and there was found to be a very considerable portion of it not to toe required or, (at least, nob to be desirable to take, -because it was crossed by roads that would have to be suppressed, and it was not considered proper that that should be done. Those were abandonedi. But when they were abandoned there was a valuation made on those lots which figured them out to be worth $13.62 an acre, and there was deducted from the price to be paid by Mr. Barr, not $12 an acre for those lots, but $13.62 an acre, which shows that those lots -and I think there were about 4,000 acres in round figures of that land-

subsubtopic: PURCHASE OF HAND FOR THE CAMP SITE.
speechtext: North of the Mad river.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: PURCHASE OF HAND FOR THE CAMP SITE.
speechtext:
Yes. As I say, there never was a purchase lat $12 an acre of the land of these 'particular people referred to at all. There was a purchase of that whole block tat a sum total price, which if you divide it toy acres, would figure out at $12 per acre; and that price was made after the most careful valuation by men of the very highest repute. The interest of the Crown to acquire that as a whole is perfectly obvious, as Mr. Justice Cassels points out in his judgment.
It is quite true that Mt. Barr did not own all the land, and it is quite true that it was agreed that whatever portion of it Mr. Barr could not acquire the Crown would; itself expropriate, ae it did itself expropriate it. We have heard something about the prostitution of the rights of the Crown. Why my hon. friend, who is a very distinguished lawyer, will quite realize that if we had not bought from Mr. Barr we would have gone out and expropriated the entire property.

subsubtopic: PURCHASE OF HAND FOR THE CAMP SITE.
speechtext: And saved money.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: PURCHASE OF HAND FOR THE CAMP SITE.
speechtext:
I ibeg the hon. gentleman's pardon. It was. precisely (because it was established to us by the valuation that I spoke of that it would be more economical for the Crown to pay this, price which these valuators stood behind than to take the chance of exaggerated values in the expropriation that the transaction was carried out in the way in which it was. And the mere stipulation-this stipulation which the hon. gentleman qualifies as prostitution of the Crown's rights-it is hard to keep serious and so describe it-that, if Mr. Barr failed to deliver to us any of the property he had undertaken to sell to us we should exercise the methods which we had of acquiring it and charge him the difference in the price. If it cost us any more to expropriate it, we would charge him the difference; if it cost us less to expropriate it, of course then we had no damage to claim from him and he took his whole original price. I would like to point out that this price all through was $207,000, the price for the entire property. We deducted from that $13.62 an acre for the acres that were abandoned, and we set off against that whatever was paid when we expropriated the property.
What was this awful thing that was said to these people who complained? Mind you, I understand the people who complained. I do not as readily understand the indigna-

tion of the hon. gentleman, to whom I give credit for having, perhaps, a clearer apprehension of the actual facts. These people were very unfortunate victims, but they were victimized when they bought, not when we acquired the property. Mr. Justice Cassels points that out in his judgment. He makes reference to "what might mildly be termed the highly coloured literature" that induced these people to buy these "blow sand" hills for orchards and all sorts of purposes which on its face would give them an extraordinary value.

subsubtopic: PURCHASE OF HAND FOR THE CAMP SITE.
speechtext: Is it not a fact that they purchased those very lots from Barr originally?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: PURCHASE OF HAND FOR THE CAMP SITE.
speechtext:
I am not aware whether they did or not. And I am not interested in the slightest degree in the question whether Mr. Barr is a saint or a sinner. What I am trying to point out is that these people, so far as this Government is concerned, got absolutely every dollar that they would have got if we had proceeded in the ordinary course to expropriate, and as we did with regard to other lands and that, they were not injured one iota, because if you figure out the total price which we were to pay Barr for the whole amount it would have been $12 per acre. We did not pay Mr. Barr anything for that acre; we charged over against the price that we were to pay Mr. Barr whatever the courts said we ought to acquire that property for at the expropriation rate. So that I fancy that if I am capable of making anything clear I have made it quite clear that under that contract there never was bought the land of those particular people at $12 an acre.
Now as to what is complained of that these people were told. In so far as Mr. Barr may or may not have said that he was the agent of the Government-if he so said I do not think he correctly described himself-but in so far as Mr. Radenhurst or anybody else told these people that if they would not accept the price that the Government offered them they would have to be subjected to expropriation, why they were told the simple truth. That is described as an awful threat. Well, it is what happens to any proprietor when for public purposes the Crown believes that it is necessary for it to take their property. These people were offered, I think, $8 an acre, which was the price mentioned with regard to these particular cases. I know a number were offered $8 an acre, and some were offered less; and som^ of the lots were

found when it went before the court to be worth less than that. If I followed correctly the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux), he was speaking of the people who did not go to court. It is very unfortunate for those people, because they were told, which was the truth, that inasmuch as the Government required that land, if they would not accept what was offered they would have to resort to expropriation proceedings. If, because they were told that, they parted with their particular properties at anything less than they were worth, that is very unfortunate. But that is something that is not peculiar to them; that is what happens to any man whose property is expropriated by the Crown when the Crown does not feel justified in offering him an amount which he is willing to accept. The cases which did go before the court, as my hon. friend has pointed out, and as the judgment of Mr. Justice Cassels which I have before me shows, demonstrated that the offers made to all of these people were, in the words of Mr. Justice Cassels, "generous offers."
His lordship deals with the question of how he is to proceed to value. He endeavours not to fail to be as liberal as a man can be, but he does not think it ^proper for him to be generous with the money of other people. He points out what I am sure both my hon. friends will riot dispute, that the mere fact that these people had bought their lands at a price vastly more than they are worth did not justify him in allowing-nor would it, I think, justify the Crown in paying-more than they were worth. Looking at the facts of the case, therefore, I fancy that my two hon. friends will realize that their indignation was at least a little over-warm. Most assuredly the Crown had no desire to do these people out of one dollar of value that they owned. Reference has been made to the fact that some of them were soldiers and that some had soldier relatives. Surely it is not suggested that that would be a reason why the Crown would not want to do them justice. We were acquiring this property on behalf of the country and it was our duty to take the best available method of securing it at a reasonable value. We did secure the entire property at a reasonable price. We acquired it as a whole and were able to deal -with it as a whole. No individual was thereby placed in any worse position than he would have been in had we exercised our undoubted Tight of expropriating without any transaction with Mr. Barr at all.
