speechtext: $75,000 might have been saved if the Crown had expropriated.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: PURCHASE OF HAND FOR THE CAMP SITE.
speechtext:
It was because of the very best advice we could get on the subject-advice to the effect that we would save a large sum of money by making the acquisition in this way-that we proceeded as we did. My hon. friend has had enough experience in expropriation proceedings to know that what has happened in this particular case is rather the exception than the rule in expropriation proceedings. If the Crown had proceeded to expropriate this entire 17,300 acres, there was danger. ot its finding itself mulcted for more than the valuation put upon it. That is the experience of most people who have had to do with expropriations. Having been in touch during the last seven or eight years with the expropriation proceedings of this Government, I know that it is only rarely that on expropriation proceedings we do not pay more than in the judgment of our valuators the property is worth. The price fixed for the land we abandoned goes to demonstrate that, for a very large proportion of it at all events, we certainly would have paid more than $12 an acre had we proceeded by expropriation. I can understand that the situation of these people is such as to command our sympathy and very easily-with a little goodwill, perhaps-to arouse the very warm feeling that has been expressed. But with the facts before us, it must be clear that no wrong or injustice has been done any party in this connection save that which was suffered by those unfortunate people when they were induced to purchase this land at absolutely fictitious prices. I hold no brief for Mr. Barr; I do not know him; I never saw him. Whether he has had anything to do with the selling of the land to these people I am not in a position to say. If he had; if he is the author of " highly-coloured literature " of Which Mr. Justice Cassels speaks, he certainly would be open to grave reprehension for his action in misrepresenting the property he was selling to these people. I do not say that he is deserving of that, because I do not know what his connection with the matter was.
The hon. gentleman has appealed to us to reconsider cases. I am not in a position to speak as to a particular case where a man made a settlement. It is, perhaps, possible that in some particular case a man took less than his property was worth because he preferred not to be expropriated. If there fce room for consideration of cases

of that kind I shall be glad to look into them. But the facts as established by the documents on the file, by the judgments of the court and by the result itself to Mr. Barr, all tend to negative the idea that anybody was deprived o'f his property without getting full value.
I hold in my hand a statement of how this thing petered out. The hon. member (Mr. Jacobs) spoke about our prostituting the powers of the Crown by lending them to Mr. Barr. What was done with regard to the lands that had .to be expropriated was this: the Crown expropriated them and charged up against Mr. Barr whatever it paid for the expropriation .

subsubtopic: PURCHASE OF HAND FOR THE CAMP SITE.
speechtext: Does my hon. friend read from the judgment of Judge Cassels?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: PURCHASE OF HAND FOR THE CAMP SITE.
speechtext:
That would not bear upon the result to Mr. Barr, but this is what Mr. Justice Cassels says, speaking of the purchasers-he had a great number of cases before him:
There are different classes of purchases of these Camp Borden lands. A considerable number of acres were laid off Into twenty acre lots, and influenced' no doubt by what might be mildly termed very highly coloured literature issued by Messrs. Wright and Barr and by Mr. Enoch Thompson, numerous people were induced to purchase these twenty-acre lots at prices averaging from $15 to $16 per acre. These purchasers, needless to say, were persons living at a distance from Camp Borden. As for /Mr. Shook, a witness much relied on by the defendants, he states in answer to a question :-
"Q.-Can you tell us what the value of these lands are, say as orchard Lands? A. Well, I can scarcely give you the value of them; from their surroundings I would not like to because the people there are pessimistic about the value of that land and do not think it worth anything.
As lands for a Camfi they may be very suitable. As lands for agricultural or fruitgrowing purposes or vegetable gardens I would agree (except as to a portion of lands in Essa Township and perhaps a small quantity of acres in Pine River flats) with the ".people there."
*He is speaking of the particular lots that he had before him, not of the entire land; and he makes his exceptions. Further on he refers to/ the prices they paid, and points out what in law and in common sense must be perfectly clear; that the value of a land is' not necessarily what a man may have been deceived into paying for it.
I was going to refer to the result of the transaction. Hon. gentlemen have spoken about an $80 profit on every lot. As I say, the process was that Mr. Barr, being credited with $207,000, was charged up with what we paid for tlje lots as we expropriated' them.

Being credited with $12 an acre, the price agreed upon with Barr, on 14,596-6 acres, or an amount of $175,159.20, the Crown charged up to Mr. Barr $138,977.04, being the amount that we paid in acquisition of the land. We also charged up to him advances made to him, amounting in all to $22,000. Those two amounts deducted from $175,159.20, leave a balance of $14,182.15 available for the acquisition of the land still remaining to be acquired, which is 490-6 acres, which at $12 an acre would amount to $5,887.20. To be deducted from that $14,182.16, is $2,818.52, being what was coming to us for the land abandoned. That is what we were entitled to charge up. Over and above dropping $12 an acre from the price for those lands, we were entitled to an additional $1.32 an acre because they were worth more than $12. There was also to be charged up an estimate on account of buildings disposed of by Barr, amounting to $1,400. That makes a total deduction of $4,218.52 to be made from $14,182.16, leaving a balance of $9,963.64 to cover the cost of the lots still to be acquired. It is to be pointed out that, in the acquisition of these lands, Mr. Barr had to incur considerable expense in connection with agents and one thing or another, so that those figures do not represent a profit going to Mr. Barr. He had to pay out of that all the expenses involved in the acquisition of such lots as he acquired or endeavoured to acquire, so that when one speaks of getting a profit of $80 a lot on those particular lots, it is quite manifest he did not. It all comes down to this, that Mr. Barr sold us a block of land at a block price, and that therefore, you cannot conclude anything ' fro'm the fact that, by dividing that amount by the number of acres, you get a price of $12 an acre, and that was so stated. You cannot deduce from that that each acre was worth $12 an acre, nor that he got $12 an acre for each acre of that immense block of *land. Not only was it shown at the time of the abandonment of the property, hut the fact was notorious to all at that time that all of this land had not an equal value, and it is quite obvious that a tract of that size would not have an equal value throughout.

speechtext:
The strangest part of this transaction, a part which has been lightly touched upon by the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. .Lemieux), and which has not been touched upon by the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Boys) or the Minister of Justice, is this: It is quite conceivable, under the circumstances de-

soiibed by the minister and by the hon. member for South Simcoe that Mr. Barr may have made a loss and not a profit on his transaction. The hon. member for Mai-sonneuve has rather conveyed to us the impression that Mr. Barr must have made a great deal of money, and it has been contended on the other side that Mr. Barr may possibly have lost money by having to pay more than $12 an acre for some portions of the land. That is quite possible, but it is not at all probable that that took place at all.	[DOT]

subsubtopic: PURCHASE OF HAND FOR THE CAMP SITE.
speechtext: I did not wish for one moment to say I thought Mr. Barr lost money, but I did say that the'figures given to me showed that the profit he made was not a profit that would induce any member of this House or any business man to interest himself in the transaction.

subsubtopic: PURCHASE OF HAND FOR THE CAMP SITE.
speechtext: I do not question that for a moment, but I think it was intended that Mr. Barr as a business man should make a profit out of the transaction. I think it will be an equally fair assumption that the Acting Minister of Militia and Defence intended that Mr. Barr should have an opportunity of making a large profit, a profit he would have to make at the expense of either the owner of the land or the public treasury. But the question that strikes me as the most extraordinary part of the matter is-why did the Minister of Militia have anything to do with Mr. Barr in regard to anything that Mr. Barr did not own? Mr. Barr owned 8,000 acres. It would be right and proper for the Minister of Militia to bargain with Mr. Barr to buy his land; but why did the Minister of Militia bargain wth Mr. Barr for land belonging to other people? The Minister of Justice said they did not buy any particular acres; that they bought from Mr. Barr a tract of 16,000 acres of land. Mr. Barr did not own that quantity of land. They bought from Mr. Barr that which he had no right to sell. They gave Mr. Barr what was in effect a license to go around all those people representing himself as an agent of the Government, make bargains with them and, in some cases, acquire land at prices which they considered were too low. If the Government had actually paid $8 an acre, I do not suppose those people would have complained. What they seem to complain of is that the Government paid $12 an acre, and they got only $8, and it is not satisfactory to say that the Government paid an average price which was fair all around. Why did they have any "Barr" in this transaction? Why was Mr. Barr brought into the matter at all? My hon. friend says the experience of the members of the Government is that expropriation proceedings generally lead to considerable cost. I agree with him in that respect. Evidently he did not need to be alarmed in this case, because we have had the expropriation proceedings carried on under the peculiar circumstances described by the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) and the judge of the Exchequer Court has placed: a low valuation on those lands- It seems that, if the case had from the beginning been taken into the Exchequer Court, a very high price could not have been allowed for those worthless sand lands or "blow sands," as my hon. friend describes them. There dia not seem to have been any danger in expropriating; but, danger or no danger, this is a method of buying land for the Government which is open to the utmost possible abuse. Why should there have been any "Barr" middleman in this transaction? Why did the Government not buy from Barr that which Barr had to sell, and in some way, by an authorized, disinterested agent, paid for his services as an agent, meet those other people and buy their land on fair terms? This is the serious error on the part of the Government-buying from Barr something he had not to sell, giving him the equivalent of a license to beat down those people and compel them' to sell their land for what seemed to them to be low prices. That part of the transaction, irrespective of gain or loss, is_open to very gTave censure.

speakeroldname: Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Minister of the Interior):
speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: THE CHRISTIAN COMMUNITY OF UNIVERSAL BROTHERHOOD.
speechtext:
Ordinarily, a Bill respecting the incorporation of a company might be spoken to, ao far as the attitude of the Government is concerned, by the Secretary of State, but as this Bill has to do with a community that has been more directly under the administration of the Interior Department, perhaps it is as well that I should say a word with regard to it. There is a measure of much importance; in some respects, it is an extraordinary measure as far as this House is concerned. There is in Western Canada a community holding, in which, a large percentage of what are commonly called Doukhobors, are the owners; they hold community rights in it, and no particular individual has any special individual asset. As everybody knows, the property of the community stands mainly in the name of one of their leaders, Mr. Peter Verigin. I believe a share of that property stands in the name of a corporation which was incorporated under the Companies' Act, and which has a name practically the same as the name intended to be given to this community, save only that the word " Limited " is added. A portion of the assets have been conveyed to that corporation. The stock of that corporation, I understand, is held by certain trustees for the benefit of the community, or if not the whole community, for the benefit of certain members of it. The purpose of this Bill appears to be to enable the whole community to organize in a corporate capacity, and to provide facilities whereby the assets of the people will be held by the whole corporation, but also whereby the communistic right of any individual in the corporation may be withdrawn and become an individual asset. I did not think Parliament would likely

'favour the principle of the incorporation of a community in so far as commercial enterprises are concerned; but as regards this community, there have been urged certain claims and certain rights which the individuals of the community might seek to exercise and which they could not exercise if some such incorporation does not take place.

subtopic: THE CHRISTIAN COMMUNITY OF UNIVERSAL BROTHERHOOD.
speechtext: What rights are they?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: THE CHRISTIAN COMMUNITY OF UNIVERSAL BROTHERHOOD.
speechtext: The right to withdraw, inasmuch as the assets are now held by Mr. Peter Verigin in the name of the community. With respect to the rights of any individual member of the community, there is no way, unless the incorporation takes place, by which an individual member of the community can withdraw from the corporation and take his place as an ordinary citizen of Canada. This is not a matter of small concern. The community numbers about 7,000 souls. The assets run into the millions of dollars, and the position of these assets, it is very strongly urged, is not by any means on as secure a basis as it should be, having regard to the rights of individual members as against the rights of the community.

While I do not object to the passing of the second reading of this Bill, I want it to be understood that I do not favour the granting of extraordinary powers to a community of this kind. I do not oppose the second reading because I am not convinced that there will be any way by which an individual may withdraw his rights and become entitled to his individual assets unless some such protection as this is afforded him.

Mr. Speaker, at six o'clock, I said I purposed to avail myself of this motion to discuss two or three questions that are of extreme importance at this stage of our country's career and in connection with the war. The first thought to which I wish to draw the attention of the House is that expressed by the London Times of yesterday in an article discussing war and condition of affairs in Europe.

Does my hon. friend
(Mr. W. F. Maclean) intend to speak to my motion?
No.
Well, the debate is not concluded. My hon. friend, from Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) intended to say something.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is entirely a matter for the hon. member for South York (Mr. W. F. Maclean); he has the floor.
My hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) had the floor. I waited for him all afternoon and I do not see any reason why the hon. gentleman should ask me to give way.
I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon.

A significant thing was stated by the London Times of yesterday in discussing the condition of the war, or the entry of the United States into the war. It was dealing with the declaration that that country, which had. refused up to recent times to concern itself with European questions, had gone into the war because it believed the rights and liberties of civilization to be ini jeopardy and is opposed to autocracy and to the military system of Germany. The London Times, in discussing that declaration yesterday said that it was the most significant political incident that has happened in the history of the world since the French revolution. We are now voting money in connection with the war and I take this opportunity to say that I also regard the entry of the United States into the war as a matter of supreme importance. We find ourselves today, a great democratic community on the American continent, joined up with the

United States in asserting the rights of civilization as against autocracy and the German military system. Mr. Balfour, when he accepted that embassy to the United States, came to America, to Canada, to this House, and what he told us constituted an appeal from the progressive, constitutional governments, especially the British government, to the democracies of America to join with them in the great struggle. Mr. Balfour spoke here for his ' government, and) for the British people, and he presented to us the view that a supreme issue had' arrived in the history of the world and that the allied countries of Europe, through the missions which came from Great Britain and France appealed to the democracies of America to assist them in this great conflict. The glory of Canada is that the Canadian democracy, a Dominion under British constitutional rule, the day that it went into this war, assumed the leadership of America in asserting the rights of democracy and in showing that it was worth our while to take part in this struggle. We have been true to that. The United States have seen that we were right; they have joined up in this struggle, and the most significant thing flowing out of this important union between the two great democracies is that the old hatred that had been developed between the original Thirteen Colonies and the Mother Country, which had been nursed and had grown, in a way, for over a hundred years, suddenly ceased, and you find to-day Britain and her Dominions and the great American republic united in giving the whole of their resources to the defence of democracy and civilization. That is the great event of this war so far, which is making more and more impression on the people, and that is the reason why I say that I think we ought to readjust our views in regard to our position on this continent. Whereas formerly there was a disagreement between the United States and the Mother Country, and Washington was the champion of the republic as against the Mother Country, you see now that Washington is identified with the old democratic principle that was asserted by Cromwell: you see a union of the principles for which Cromwell and Washington stood, you . see Lloyd George as the leader of the English democracy, and men like Mr. Balfour claiming a connection with Lincoln and Wilson in a way that surprises all the world. That is a great advance, and it shows a new unity and a new strength on the part of democracy: you see the 
LTnited States asserting ii and ourselves asserting it, and putting all our resources into this war.
Are wre living true to it?

We are trying to do our best, but perhaps we have not done as well as we might have done. Still, we are now putting all our resources into the war, and the reason we are going to win eventually, and the reason we are going to win the world to our view, is the existence of this new condition that has brought about so great a change. What is the one thing that the German Kaiser failed to allow for, and failed to make any calculation in regard to? He never believed that the - democracies of Europe and America would be united; he never believed that the United States and Britain would go hand in hand, and he thought he could defy the United States and could defy Britain; and the one thing he is up against now is this new and powerful union.
In view of that union between Great Britain and the United States, would my hon. friend revise his view's and ideas about the reciprocity treaty?

That is always in the hon. gentleman A mind. I stood on the floor of this House and defended, and am prepared now to defend, my record in regard to reciprocity. I was -the first man in this House, session after session, to demand, for public reasons, the free entrance of the wheat products of the Canadian West into the United States-
Mr. LEMIEUxk'feut not in 1911.
-and Canada is to-day the leader of democracy in America, except that in that reciprocity issue we decided to keep our independence on this continent. '
Will the hon. gentleman define in what way the reciprocity treaty interfered with our independence?
I will answer the hon. gentleman.
Speak, for the farmers are listening.
It is very easy to answer.
Sidetracked.
I am not sidetracked, and I cannot be sidetracked on an issue of that kind.
Oh, oh.
Wait a minute. I hope the hon. gentleman will listen to me.

Certainly.
Mr. W. F. iMACLEAN: I am not in the habit of interrupting the hon. gentleman when he is making an argument. At any time that he presents arguments he is listened to by the House. Why are we going to win this war? Because we have united and consolidated our efforts and our resources, and this is the surprising thing that the Kaiser never counted upon. The great American Republic has put into this struggle the resources of the great Mississippi valley-ail their vast industrial resources; and we in Canada have put in the resources of the great Saskatchewan plains, with all their food products, and now we find that Germany will not be able to maintain against the consolidated Ameri-* can democracy their insolent assertion that civilization must how to them, that the rights of smaller peoples must yield to them, that German military power must govern the world. Now that- we have reached the point where all the resources of the United States and of Canada are bound together a new view has come to the people of America ito this extent: They know now-and this is what I want to impress upon the House-that the continent of America to-day is the home of democracy, it is the place where the battle of democracy has to be fought, the place from which the food and all the resources to uphold democracy must come. That is why the United States have gone into the struggle, that is why they aTe putting all their resources into the fight, and that is why we are going to win. And, as I say, we of Canada, and the people of the United States, must take a new view and make a new alignment in regard to these great world questions. A while ago we would have said that our whole case for democracy and for the rights of civilization was our connection with the Mother Country. That was true, but it is still more true now that the rights of democracy depend more and more on these new political forces that have come together and that [DOT] are asserting themselves in this great war. We *must realize that to-day America, the midcontinent, the continent that by its Atlantic aspect looks on Europe, and by its *Pacific outlook, takes Asia in view; America, the centre ef the world and the
centre of democracy, with that outlook, and with its resources controls the situation, and if it believes-as it does believe- in democracy, then we shall win. We have a great cause to vindicate, because, as all now admit, this war is not a European war, it is a world-wide war against German autocracy, and German domination It is a struggle into which America has entered, and which America has got to win, and practically the appeal in France and in Britain to-day is to America, " Come over and help us." And America has responded. Now, that is a matter of the greatest moment to democracy, and Canadians must fake it in that light. There has been preached in this country the doctrine of what was called " The Round Table." We have heard a good deal of that Round Table, and that organization in England which was trying to educate us, and to lead us into what they call an Imperial Federation, in which Canada-if *the idea were carried out as they proposed it-might lose her identity, and become one in some kind of confederation in which this country would have a certain number of votes as against a great many others. I am rising here to-night to object to anything of that kind, and I say that Canada must maintain her autonomy, her system of having a free voice in all these matters. And inasmuch as America hereafter is to have the controlling voice as to democracy, we must be careful that we do not drift into a system by. which we might have our liberties restricted if we connected ourselves too closely with the political organizations of Europe, and especially with a political organization, perhaps an Imperial Confederation, as has been proposed to us by the Round Table organization in Britain. Not only that, but if the resources of America are now all devoted to this war, and there is to be great new adjustment, and if peace is to be maintained after this war, it must be done from America. And if there is to be a peace police, which is the ambition now of the most progressive men who are discussing this waT, if there is to he a peace patrol, a police organization to keep down organizations like that of the German Kaiser, it i6 going to be in America and we will be part of it, and we want a very free hand in very considerable degree in regard to what we are to commit ourselves to in the future construction of the British Empire. My contention is that, instead of committing ourselves to a system of Imperial federation, we had better keep our autonomy as it is, remain in the Em-

pire as one of the Dominions of the Empire, but not to commit ourselves. And we are being invited to commit ourselves, and speeches of a certain trend that I do not .quite agree with have been made in England in connection with this war. I want to discuss that matter or call public attention to it as I a-m doing now, and to see that Canada keeps her position and her autonomy on this continent free, to join with the other Dominions of the British Empire and with the British constitutional organization as it is, and with the great American Republic.
Mr. LEM'IEUX:	Hear, hear.
That is dangerous.

Does my hon.
friend, the late Minister of Militia, not think that we should have supreme control -of the Canadian forces as the other Allies have?
I was merely saying that it was dangerous to hear the applause coming from the direction it is. I have had it myself, unfortunately.
That is good1 Liberal common sense.

Sometimes Liberals do not talk common sense. Since the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lem-ieux) has referred to this .question, I would ask what is the one reason why there was a certain holding back in the province of Quebec in regard to the great war and the

participation of Canada in it? It was probably the suspicion the people of Quebec had that they would be led into some kind of European alliance which perhaps later on would prove objectionable to them. I believe the new view of it to the province of Quebec-and I want to congratulate that province on the splendid wave of patriotism sweeping over it now, .and on the way its young men are coming forward and enlisting; they are going over as much from this Dominion as from America to maintain the liberties andi the civilization of Europe-

We will follow you as
long as you talk that way.

The ideas of
what the Empire ought to be have been expressed, as I said before, by a kind of mediaeval Round Table, and they have a great propaganda out, and they are preparing a program for us of what the future Canada ought to be in regard to conditions in Europe and questions of that kind. I do not prefer that we should be led into these proposals ox accept! them in any sense until we discuss them fully in this country, know what they are, and whither they lead. I think I am fully justified by reason of what has taken place. A word of warning should be spoken in this House on this great issue, and the people of Canada and of America should say now that inasmuch as civilization and the liberties of the world and democracy are at stake, and that the Kaiser of Germany, if he had his will, would destroy not only the liberties of Britain and of France but-the liberties of America as well, we ought to take that wider and greater view and keep our autonomy and our resources and our organizations here, ready to join with all the other British democracies and with the United States, and to recognize at last that with America-free Amerioa, that America which has made itself the dictator of the world, that America which to-day controls the situation by reason of the magnificent resources of the Mississipppi basin and plains of the Saskatchewan- we must use all our powers to maintain the liberties of the world, and are not to be inveigled into any arrangement, even if we call it an Imperial confederation, in which we do not have absolute liberty to decide what we are to do. When I say that, I am only re-echoing the statement of Sir John A. Macdonald constantly repeated in this House, that above all things, while Canada was associated with the Empire and with the Mother Country he, for one, wished that Canada should

always retain her autonomy, and that when she spoke in any Imperial gathering she would go there free, not to be governed by a vote of them all, but go as a free [DOT]Government to express her assent or dissent and to withdraw if she saw fit and to keep her autonomy and independence on every matter.
The dreams of the Kaiser have been suddenly dispelled. He finds that this great free, democratic America is organized against him. He sees the handwriting on the wall; he knows that he will not succeed. Millions of Americans are being sent to the front; all the resources of the United States are being brought to bear against the enemy. Who, having read the farewell speech of General Washington, would have imagined that the United States navy would go to Europe in defence of the liberties of Europe? But it has happened-and the Kaiser did not expect it. We have maintained our sea supremacy; Britain and France and the dominions of the Empire have held the Germans back, on the western front. I do not think Germany will succeed, and that is why I believe that this country ought to make use of all its resources to carry on the conflict. Our people ought to stand for conscription; our farmers ought to stand for it. We should put everything we have into this war, into the maintenance of the rights of democracy. I sympathize a great deal with the farmers' deputation which is in the city to-day, but I am strongly of the opinion that our farmers must do their share of the fighting as well as of the production, as I believe the Prime Minister told them to-day. The farmers having been told that production is almost equal to military service, the Government must expedite their enumeration of the man-power of the country not engaged in war, and if the farmers are unable to reap their harvests the Government must find a way to get them all the assistance they can from those now engaged in unnecessary occupations. With the enforcement of the -Military Service Act, there must go registration, conscription and a direction of the man-power of the country, in order that persons engaged in unnecessary occupations shall assist the farmers and take up any war work that has to be done. We have made some headway; it has taken a long while, but we have got that far. I believe that the farmers will accept this decision of the Government and that they will allow their boys to go. I know that they are going from my part of the country. We are presenting a united front

Canada, the overseas dominions, the Mother Country, the United States-in upholding the liberties of the world against the dominion of Germany.
In making this fight against the common ene-my we have to -alter some of our economic laws. The United -States is becoming not only the strongest factor in the war, but the nation of greatest financial resources. This financial strength of the United States is practically d-ue to their national system of currency and of banking. I have advocated on the floor of this House-and I advocate now, with still more fervour-that we should not let this -session pass; that we should not let this war pass, until we have established the strongest possible financial organization. Immediately on the outbreak of war we should have had a national currency instead of a bank currency; a national system of banking such as they have in the United States, a -great system of re-dis-counting by national banks. The United States by the adoption of this system, has stood the great strain of the war, spent -billions of money, and kept down the rate of interest. We have to go to the United- States for assistance in the matter of credit and money, and it is time that we put ourselves in good standing with them by following their example in the matter of currency and banking system. I make no objection to the Canadian -banks or to what they are doing for the building up of the country. They are doing all right, but they are working under an obselete system which ought to be -modernized-, especially in view of our position on the American continent. If we had taken steps in thi-s direction we should have been able to do a great deal more, than we have done. The -proo-f of my contention is found- in the fact that the moment Britain went into the war she adopted some of the methodis which have been adopted in the United States, Leading bankers of England in recent meetings affirmed that before the waT is over Great Britain will have to revolutionize further her system of banking and currency and follow that of the United States-, -and if it is necessary there, it is necessary here as well. If we had a national currency instead of a bank-note currency, the rate of exchange as between this country and the United State-s would not to-day be against us, and the discounting of our bank notes in the United- States -would not prevail. In so-m-e cases it is two per cent; in some cases our notes are not taken- at all, although they are just as good as United States notes. For years we have accepted notes of the

United States amounting to millions, constituting practically a loan from the Canadian people to them, and we have not had a corresponding advantage. I had hoped that the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White), who is not now in. this country, would have taken steps this session looking to the esta/blishment of a national currency and a national system of hanking such as they have in the United States.
I am not going to touch on the tariff, but I am going to touch on one thing in connection with the war. The war has clearly proved that a pastoral people, when its liberties are assailed, is quite able to take caTe of itself. Every nation, in order to maintain its liberties when they are threatened, must see to it that hereafter it is not only able to produce food, but is highly organized industrially. It must be just as strong a people as is the strongest nation in this war, that is, Great Britain. I am not asserting that as a reason for a tariff or for protection; but the new view that will sweep the North American continent is that any country that thinks it is its duty to uphold democracy and to fight for the liberties of the world must have universities with men highly qualified in the technicalities and sciences, and most of all, its education must be such that -it will turn out not only soldiers, but scientists, professors, engineers and other skilled men who will be able to organize and utilize the resources of the country for the maintenance of its liberties.. We must have factories, iwe must have engineers, we must have mechanics, we must have a high organization of our industries, we must have diversity of employment. The United States, which has all these things, is our neighbour, and while I am not, for one moment, advocating anything in the direction of protection, one of the great lessons of this war in which we are now engaged and in which we are putting our all is that we .should have our industries organized to the fullest extent.
The people of Canada feel that in this great war the transportation of the country must and ought to be nationalized. The day that Great Britain went into the war she nationalized, her railways. The day that the United States went into the war the railways of that country were practically nationalized. When we went into the war we should have nationalized out railways. We are now in process of doing it partially. If the war is to continue-and it is not over yet-it is not too late to begin,

and I hope the Government will, in a day or two, be in a position to announce to this House that they are entering upon a policy of nationalizing all the railways. I have no sympathy with the legislation recently passed in this House that out of the profits of the Canadian Pacific we shall take a percentage which shall be devoted to war purposes. How much of that is contributed by the people of Canada in increased freight rates? I do not believe that is the right way to use the railways in.
9 p.m. order to help to win the war, and I regret that the Government advanced the freight rates, instead of boldly, at the beginning of the war, taking over the. railways. By taking over the railways they could have affected consolidation and co-ordination, and, consequently, economies, which would have made possible a reduction in freight rates-and the greatest relief and encouragement that the farmers of the West can receive is to have the freight rates reduced to the lowest possible limit.
It had been my hope that by this time we should have a national system of railways, a national telegraph system and a national telephone system; that the telegraphs and telephones would be centred in the national post office, and that the central life of every community, large or small, would be in the national railway station and the national post office. If you had that, you would have in every little village, in every big town and city this splendid institution which would be the centre of national life and service. I had hoped that we would have in the Union Government a Postmaster General with instructions from his colleagues that the telegraphs and the telephones were to be taken over and concentrated with the post office and the railway ticket office in each community; that a good salary would be paid to the man or woman in charge of the office, and that it would be kept open night and day if the business of the community warranted that being done. The war would have given us a pretext for entering upon a policy of nationalization. But the war has been going on now for four years, and we have not got very far yet in nationalizing our railways. But we are making some headway.
I hope the Government will tell us that they are going to take such further steps as are necessary to the establishment of the conditions I have indicated. We have been delayed a long time in getting national railways. Those of us who years ago advocated the nationalization of our railways

did not think it would ever arrive, but like [DOT]other unexpected things, it is beginning to arrive. I appeal to the ministers from the West that we have right away in this country national railways, run absolutely free from politics, and with the main object to create a great central service in every community and to give service to the people. We should have started with taking over the Canadian Pacific. I do not believe the Canadian Pacific Railway Company will ever again have an opportunity of getting what they could get now, during war time, for that organization coming in as the foundation of a national system of railways. But they have seen fit to maintain their independence. If I interpret aright the speech delivered the other day by Lord Shaugh-nessy, it was an intimation to the people of Canada that if they wanted to take over the Canadian Pacific for war purposes or anything else, they would have to pay $200 for $100 worth of shares; or, what is the same thing, guarantee the shareholders ten iper cent. I am not prepared to say that I would guarantee the shareholders of the Canadian Pacific ten per cent. I would be quite willing to see them guaranteed eight per cent, if the road was made the backbone of a great national system of railways-. Sir Adam Beck in his proposal to electrify the railways of Canada, and especially of Ontario, should have included not only the Grand Trunk and any railways the Government may take over, but the Canadian Pacific as well. I am sure that if we had a great national system of railways we should be stronger for war purposes- and stronger for the development of our own country.
While on this question I would point out that Lord Shaughnessy, and the management of the Grand Trunk Railway who have spoken about the amount they have invested in railways in Canada, have also invested largely in railways in the United States, and when they appealed to the Canadian people to do certain things in this war they forgot to tell us that only one-fifth of the mileage of the great Canadian Pacific Railway had been taken over and is controlled to-day by the government of the United States. One-fifth of the mileage of the Grand Trunk has also passed out of the hands of the road, and is now under the control of the United States government. Inasmuch as the American government have taken over the portions of these roads lying in the United States we should' take over what is left in Canada, and then with portions of Canadian roads under the control of the United States government and
the balance under the control of our government a great continental system of transportation would evolve. That is coming. I will never believe that the American government will give up the control of those roads. The whole tendency is in the direction of public ownership, and as we are taking over some of the railways in this country we ought to take over them all and nationalize them. We ought to urge on the people and government of the United States, and on our people and our Government, that private ownership of railways is not in the public interest.
There is one other thing I should like 'to touch on, which concerns the war and is on the line of democracy, and tha; is the presence in Canada of an irresponsible Senate. The time has come-certainly now that we are engaged in war-when the Senate as constituted in this country must cease. Th-e people of the United States, if they believe in anything, believe in electing representatives -responsible to the people, and their Senate is responsible to the people through election by the State legislatures. There is no such thing in that country as an irresponsible Senate, nor has there ever been made in any other country, but this is a declaration such as I am told was made in another place in Ottawa not long ago, that the Senate of Canada was the custodian and protector of vested interests in this country. It is the people of Canada who has the right to. say what are and what are not vested interests, and the people, as an outcome of -the war, want a reorganized Senate which will be a responsible body, and then democratic principles will obtain throughout -the whole organization of Government in this country.
Does the hon. gentleman mean to say that the .appointment of Senators should come under the Civil Service Commission?

I did not say
anything of the kind, and I hope the hon. gentleman has never said- anything so foo-lish. I said the Senate of Canada should be responsible to the people of Canada. Does the hon. gentleman object to that?
No.

I hope I have
the support of the ho-n. gentleman when I say the -Senate of Canada should be reorganized. They are reorganizing the House of Lords in Great Britain. England is the most progressive country in the world, so far as putting into practice democratic

principles is concerned. A report has been made to the British H-ouse that the hereditary principle in the House of Lords must be abolished, and that the interests of the nation demand that the people should be represented not only in the House of Commons but in the House of Lords as well.
Mr. RICHA1RD18ON:	Can the hon. gentleman tell us something about that report?

All I know is that Lord Bryce presented a report in the British Parliament the other day recommending the reconstitution of the House of Lords, and that the hereditary principle and the domination of the House by the aristocratic families should be wiped out.

Hear, hear.
Mr. iV. F. MACLEAN: My hon. friend says "Hear, hear." He supported a party for many years that could have accomplished a similar reform in our Senate, but I am not blaming him so much.
I was young.

Youth is no cloak for wrong views. I say that, inasmuch as they are reorganizing parliamentary institutions in England and making them more progressive; inasmuch as the American republic has representative institutions and has no hereditary principle in their Senate -and life appointments are the next thing to hereditary appointments, and we have life appointments in this country-the people of Canada not only demand the reforms I have urged to-night, but they want Senate reform fight away so as to give us a parliamentary organization that will be truly democratic.
I have asked the attention of hon. members for a short time, but I thought it was my duty on this occasion to say that inasmuch as we are engaged in a war we ought to take a new view of the war-the American and democratic view. We should have more national organization in this country; the nationalization of our railways and telegraphs; we should have Senate reform, and banking reform and a national currency. We cannot get all these things at once, but we ought to set our hearts on some of them and go after them. We have now a Union Government, and as we are in a position to deal with Civil Service reform and things of that kind, we ought to deal with these greater questions, and deal with them in the presence'of this great war.

speechtext:
I had intended to say a few words on the motion of my hon. friend from Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux), but as I have just been trying to follow the meanderings and excursions of my hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean), perhaps I had better say a word first on the very interesting discussion in which as usual the hon. member has indulged. For-* tunately or otherwise, there are usually long intervals between the deliverances of the hon. member. His deliverances are always exactly the same.
But they are exactly the same. There is not the slightest conceivable difference between them, but by reason of the fact that they are not 'delivered very close together they are always more or less interesting. I think a man finds the Ten Commandments almost interesting when he reads them over, but they are ancient literature. I would rather think, without meaning the slightest offence, that the speeches of the hon. member smack somewhat of the Ten Commandments in so far as ancient literature is concerned.
Mr. W. F. MiACLEAN: They are good Commandments, and- the hon. gentleman might well observe them.

There was one part of his speech that struck me as somewhat interesting, and that was the part of it in which he was so strongly in favour of reciprocity. He was a strong reciprocity man and emphatic in the assertion that intercourse should exist between ourselves and the United States. It just occurred to me that perhaps the hon. gentleman was getting out his flying topsails for the time when the reciprocity gale passes over. He rigs his little Tory craft and trims it to the breeze when it is necessary to carry him through the Tory storms and to bring him safely to the Tory harbour. But when that passes away and when we come to the blue skies of common sense and free breathing in regard to trade again, he pulls out these old sails that he has temporarily stowed away and plays around with them again. But, from time to time, when anything like a storm appears on the horizon, this, the most agile sailor who ever trimmed his sails to meet Tory conditions, is again on the yard-arm and his little Tory oTaft is fitted out- and made ready to carry him to a safe haven.
The hon. member was talking to the farmers who are here to-night. I did not intend

195ff>
to say anything had he not invited me into that realm of discussion. It is exceedingly interesting to me as a farmer-(not a fanner now, but a farmer's son brought up on the farm-to see the farmers around here. It reminds' me of home and friends and the conditions of my early days. I have the greatest sympathy with and respect for the men who come here looking for their rights and a hearing of their case. The hon. member for South York told us the reason why they were here. I do not think he made the reason why they are here plain enough.
I will tefll him why they are here. I wish my hon. friend would torn his mind hack to the third day of December last when there was something going on in this, country in which he was interested. While he, no doubt, was practically secure in his county, I imagine that he still had an interest in his friends making a safe harbour, and I have no doubt he had a hand in passing this Order in Council. Here it is:
His Excellency the Governor General in Council, on the recommendation of the Rt. Hon. Sir Robert Laird Borden, the Prime Minister, and under and in virtue of the provisions of The Military Service Act, is pleased1 to order and it is hereby ordered that in any case where a person engaged in agriculture has applied for exemption and such exemption has been refused-the Minister of Militia and Defence, if he is of the opinion that the services of such person are essential for promoting agricultural production may, by order under his hand, discharge such person from military service.
That was the promise that was made to the farmers of Ontario.

The hon. gentleman
quotes there the simple fact that "if he is of the otpinion," which implies "if he is not of opinion" as well.

This Order in Council speaks clearly and distinctly for itself. I have the greatest respect for the outbreaks of the hon member for West Peterborough (Mr. Burnham) and I must say we are never sure as to where he is going to break out next. But, I have greater respect for the deliberations of Union Government. When, - acting together and in the name of the Governor General, they reach a certain conclusion and put that in writing and publish it to the world, I prefer to take that as against the hon. member for West Peterborough. Because of the necessity of encouraging production to wipe aside the Military Service Act and make provision for the exemption o<f men engaged in agriculture, every Tory candidate in the province of Ontario from the third of December until election-day preached the doctrine:
"Come unto me all ye that labour and are' heavy laden and I will give you rest; my yoke is easy and my burden is light; po-body shall go to the war if he comes to me and supports the Tory candidate in the province of Ontario; this doctrine of conscription is intended for Quebec; it is a Quebec nostrum; it is not for you; you have done all you should do; this Order in Council is to let you out and- to bring in the-men from the province of Quebec and elsewhere; therefore, do not be afraid, come and vote for us and we will do you good." Well, the Government found themselves elected. They found that these farmers in Ontario voted1 for them and now they say to the farmers: "We are here and you are there; we have no further use for you as voters, we want your sons for the front and to the front they shall go." The farmers of Ontario are reasonable and sensible men and when a farmer in Ontario or elsewhere promises a thing it means that he is going to do it. This Union Government, or the Government of the day, promised that they were going to exempt the farmers' sons and the people of Ontario believed that that was true. Because they are insisting on that promise is why they are here to-day, if the hon. gentleman (Mr. W. F. Maclean) did not know it. And I hope they will be successful in impressing upon the Government the weight and force of a promise. When the name of the Governor General and the name of His Majesty are introduced into a promise and when that promise is published in the form of an Order in Council which has the force of a statute, the Government, I hope, will think seriously before they forsake their promise, ot treiat it as a "scrap of paper," or take the position before the country that they are not bound by it. That is about all I propose to say with respect to the speech of my hon. 'friend. There is no man in the House or in the country who can speak with greater ease upon general questions when we are at a safe distance from an election. But when he gets close up to the wind a chicken never ran under its mother's wing quicker than the hon. member gets under the wing of the old Tory hen.

Now, my purpose in- addressing you this evening, Mr. Speaker, was to offer a few observations in connection with this Camp Borden land purchase.

The Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), who is not here this evening, amused me rather this afternoon in discussing this very innocent case of land purchase that he found at Camp Borden, which is situated somewhere in the vicinity of the town of Barrie in the county of Simcoe. It is marvellous, Mr. Speaker, the extremely innocent cases that the Minister of Justice will find. I was trying to think out for myself some other conceivable purchase of land that could by any possibility be as innocent as this purchase of the site of Camp Borden, and being .somewhat of a Biblical scholar, my mind reverted to the fact that Adam had a piece of land in which he was cultivating trees. I have no doubt he bought that land from somebody, I do not know who it was, and as he bought it in the days of his innocence, before he took to dealing in apples, I have every reason to believe that it was a most innocent transaction, perhaps the most pure and stainless transaction that ever took place in the world up to this; tout, nevertheless, as compared with the innocence, beauty and purity, the crystal-like brightness of this transaction at Camp Borden, it is dark and forbidding. Perhaps the Minister of Justice made himself believe that everything in connection with this transaction was innocent. Let us ask ourselves first the question, why was this man Barr bothering with the thing at all if it was the child-like transaction that it is sought to be made out? If there was no money to be made out of the deal, why were the great money-making barons of the city of Toronto bothering with it? We find in connection with this sale of land names which suggest transactions which are somewhat lucrative. We find that this agreement was likely made in the office of the National Trust Company, because one of the men connected with that company is a witness,-one name I find on the contract is that of Mr. Poucher, of the National Trust Company. The same man, Mr. Poucher, witnesses the signature of Sir Edward Kemp, evidently in the office of the National Trust Company. Apparently too, Mr. Barr is present in the office, because the same gentleman witnesses his signature also. Knowing who the directors of the National Trust Oom-'pany are, I realize that they would not be playing with a matter of this kind unless there was some money in it. I am informed, Sir, by a gentleman from Toronto -I am not vouching for the statement which was sent to me in writing over the signature of a certain man who- may be, 
and I have no doubt is, a respectable resident of that city-that $60,000 or $90,000 cold cash wa3 made out of this transaction, and if the National Trust Company, and the other parties mentioned that appear in connection with this agreement had anything to do with it I can well believe they would not bother with any matter in which much less money was made.
If I correctly remember the statement ot the Minister of Justice, he said there was nothing in the papers which would indicate that there was a guarantee of $12 an acre for Mr. Barr. If he did not say that, or if Hansard does not show that to be correct, my statement will have to be regarded as not having been uttered, because I am' basing my assertion on my recollection of what the hon. gentleman said. The agreement, however, discloses that the statement of the Minister of Justice is not correct. That there was such a guarantee is disclosed by the agreement which I find on page 2 of a pamphlet *which was sent t,o me. The agreement, which is signed by Hon. Mr. Kemp and by Mr. Barr, and is dated April, 1916, declares that Mr. Barr is to have $12 an acre for the land, whether he can buy it for that price or buy it for less, and he is not to pay for the cost of any expropriation proceedings. If it was found necessary to go to court a condition of the agreement is that Air. Barr is not to pay any. costs. He is sure of $12 an acre, and the Government undertakes to pay whatever it cost to expropriate the land. I submit to yoiu, Mr. Speaker, that that is not a fair proposition. If Mr. Barr had land of his own that he wished to sell, as the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) said, it was perfectly right and proper for him to give the Government an option on it and to state how much he would take; but, as far as the rest of the agreement is concerned, I submit it is an absolutely new and novel procedure-at any rate it is absolutely new and1 novel to me. I never heard before of a man going to any Government and saying, "You want to buy a certain area of land, I have some land that I will sell you, and I know where some more land is to be got; I do not own a foot of it, but I will try to buy it, and if I do I will sell it to you at a profit. If I cannot buy the land you will expropriate it for me, and I will sell it to you at a profit.'' That, in brief, constitutes the agreement, and it is one of an extraordinary character. It is a transaction that should be fully

sifted, and upon which the full light of day should be thrown.
Now what happened, and was this transaction fair to the poor men who owned the land? The hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Boys) said that a man should not get for land all that he paid for it. Well, I have had a good deal of experience in connection with the expropriation of land and I have never heard, until this extraordinary case came before us, of any man who sold land getting less for it than he had paid. As a rule, you go up against the Government; you show them your titles and the price of your land. You say: " There is a piece of land; I paid $20 an acre for it;
I do not want- to sell it at all; you are taking it from me; is it not li'ttle enough for you to give me what I paid for it?" Most men representing the Government would say: " That seems to be a fair proposition, it does not look out of the way; so long as we are satisfied you paid that for it, we will give you that amount." That is what these poor men would have got for their land but for the interference of Barr. It was to his interest to beat down this price and get as much below $12 as he could, and he, no doubt, corralled into that court and brought to bear upon that judge all the sharpers he could gather round him to run down the price of that land, and they got it well below $12, and that enabled him to make a profit. I submit, jSir, that there is nothing of the square deal about that. It looks to me as if there was an understanding by which those representing the Government entered into an arrangement with Barr for the purpose of helping him out, and what was to be done with the money at the heel of the hunt I do not know. All the information and evidence we have is that Barr received all of this money, but we do know on accasions it does happen that in transactions of this kind more people benefit than those whose names appear upon the surface. And I do submit to the Government and to you, Sir, that transactions of this kind should not be permitted to pass without some notice; that when the Public Works and other departments of this country want land they should have the courage to go straight to the owners themselves and make their own bargains, and if they cannot make a straight bargain themselves, if they cannot get the land for the price they think is fair, then the Exchequer Court exists, and they can go there and fight the thing out" openly before the people. If they do that the people will stand with them and have greater satisfaction than if they play a 124
hide-and-seek game of some kind through a middleman. The people of this country are not anxious to do business in that way, they are anxious to do business in a straightforward, square manner in the open market. Although my hon. friend from Simcoe (Mr. Boys) spoke very highly of the solicitor whose name appeared in this affair-and I have no doubt in the world but that he is as excel-jent a man as he is represented to be- nevertheless in a letter written by that gentleman on November 25, 1916, there are two inaccuracies. In the first place, he holds up this man Barr as the agent of the Government which he is not, and says he is the purchasing agent of the Government, which he is not. He says:
I enclose you herewith the formal tender on belhalf of the Crown for the lands expropriated as part of Camp Borden.
The tender which Mr. Barr made was not on behalf of the Crown but on behalf of himself. He was trying to get the land himself and sell it to the Crown, and any tender he made was not on behalf of the Crown. Another statement in this letter is misleading. He says later on:
The Crown is only anxious that what Is fair and just shall be done, but as the purchasing agent and you differ as to values, this is the only course we see that can be fairly taken to ascertain the value of the lands.
So far as I can gather there never was a purchasing agent of the Government who went to the owner of the land at all, except the man who went for the purpose of getting the land for himself. If any further proof were necessary to show that this land was to be $12 an acre to Mr. Barr, no matter whether he bought it for $1 or more from the owners, I quote from page 6 of the reasons for judgment given by the Judge of the Exchequer Court:
It was strongly and repeatedly pressed during the course of the trial that the Crown having agreed to pay Barr $12 an acre for his lands and those to be acquired by him is estopped from disputing the fact that the market value of the lands is at least $12 an aore.
The judge found there was an agreement by which Barr was to" get $12, and there is no question about that at all. He said so; it appears in the evidence, and the judge so finds. I repeat that statement because I understand that the Minister of Justice stated that it was improper for us to make the argument that this man had a fixed price oi $12 an acre. I say, Sir, and I do not want to take any more of the time of the House, that this is a transaction which



should not have taken place; that powers were placed1 in Barr that should never have been placed in him; that agents and men were used to get hold of this land and to make a big profit for the middleman, to the detriment and disadvantage of the owners of the land. I am glad that the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) brought this matter up, and that it has been aired in the House, and I believe that letting daylight in on these things will have a tendency to cheek departments from getting entangled in shady transactions of this kind in the future.

I wish to express my sympathy with the large numlber of people whose property was virtually confiscated in this Camp Borden undertaking. I have had many letters 'and a great number of declarations from these people, and it was stated this afternoon by the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Boys) that the real estate men a short time before subdivided into ten or twenty acre farms a great deal of this property, and it was virtually exploited1 by these real estate men; and in that way these people were induced to purchase land at an exorbitant price. I do not agree with that statement. There were many acres of land there that were sold at a price that the people were satisfied to pay, which ran at $10, $15 andi $20 an acre. But if these real estate men were accused of exploiting that territory, what about those who came after and exploited it from those people or confiscated the property they were satisfied with? I have been over many hundreds of acres of land that was so condemned. There are some parts of it, as has been stated, with drift sand on it; there are other parts with considerable forest, good land and splendid running streams. For those people who purchased that land with the intention to build bungalows, or summer homes and who did not want to farm, it was perfectly satisfactory. I will admit that if a farmer had to occupy that land as farm land with the idea of making money out of it, he would perhaps have had difficulty with it. But for the purpose most of them purchased it, for it was worth all they paid for it. Then if these exploiters who came after and said the land was only worth $3, $7 and $8 an acre-and it has been suggested by the hon. member for South Simcoe that they paid m some cases more than |12 an acre; perhaps they did, but they had to make that up by squeezing the smaller men to get it down to an average-they did that with the men who had

no other alternative, on a threat, than to give up their holdings at a great sacrifice. Why should they have been treated in that way when it is admitted that while many got very good prices, others did not get anything like what the property cost them? I believe that the Government had no desire. that these peopl-e should receive that treatment.
Apparently somebody who was on the inside took advantage of the Government and exploited this land. I consider that these people who sacrificed the earnings of many years in order to purchase this property have a grievance. They feel that the matter ought to be gone into. If, according to the various declarations and communications sent to members of this House, it is evident that these people have been taken advantage of by agents of the Government, then the Government should make good. If, on the other hand, the Government was not responsible for these agents, who, perhaps, got an inside inkling that quantities of land would be required, then it is not for the Government to make good. It is said that some gentleman connected with this transaction had eight thousand acres of land. The question is, did he own that some years previous to this transaction, or did he become the possessor of it at this particular time? It looks as if he must have got some inside information which caused him to secure certain land. To make the transaction complete he had to get other lands and even had to do considerable squeezing. A statement has been made on the floor of the House that a considerable profit was realized out of these speculations by some person at the expense of the poor people who were not in a position to go to the courts and fight their cases. Some of those who were able to go to the courts and fight their cases got better prices than those who were not in a position to do so but had to give up, you might say, under threat.
I wish to read another case which has not been brought to the attention of the House and which will show the position in which some of the people were placed. Not merely one or two but quite a large number have the same grievance. This appears to be one of the extreme cases where advantage was taken of a person who was not in a position to fight his case. The following is the declaration of David McClelland, of Toronto:
I,	David McClelland, of the city of Toronto, in the County of York, do solemnly declare:
1. That in August, 19IK5, I purchased 20 acres in Tosorontio for live hundred ($500) :

I paid seventy dollars ($70) on account of purchase and undertook in wrtting to pay four hundred and1 thirty dollars ($430) the balance thereof.
2.	That I expended the sum of $731.20 in cash on said lands for lumber and materials for a dwelling house which I erected thereon and outbuildings, and for clearing and fencing said lands.

That said lands with Others were on the 11th day of May 1916, expropriated for the purpose of a military camp or training ground for soldiers and now called "Gamp Barden," though I got no notice of such expropriation and knew nothing whatever of my having to give up the lands until I was called upon by Mr. Wright (of Messrs. Wright and Barr, real estate agents, Toronto) who told me that Mr. Barr had purchased my interests in said lands from a Mr. (Smith who had sold the land to me and that the lands had been expropriated by the Government for the purpose of a military camp, and he offered' me $200 for my title therein, saying if I did not take that sum I might get nothing iat all, but later on he sent me word, to meet him at Barrie where he, through Sir, Radenhurst, the Government solicitor, served me with a notice, offering me $300 for said lands.
4.	That my family were living in said house on the lands and in the latter end of July, 1916, we were told to get out and away or we would be shot as we were in the firing line, and were compelled1 to leave, and after taking the furniture away I went back for the window hanging and floor mgs left behind but the house had in my absence been partly broken down and the rugs, etc., taken away and I was refused permission to take away anything further off said lands.
'5. Thiat in the expropriation proceedings before the Honourable Sir Walter Cassels I claimed $1,810 including my cash payments for my expenditure in material and labour in fencing and preparing said lands for crop, for loss of season's crops, and for compensation for trouble, inconvenience and expense in moving to and from said lands.

That the Honourable Sir Walter Oassels heard the evidence but though I testified to my expenditure of $7311.20 and asked him to look at. my receipts therefor, he refused to do so, saying he was appointed to try the value of the land on the lllth of May, 1916, and afterwords gave his award for the $300 offered me, and I was to pay my own costs, which amounted to $130 leaving me a balance of $170 in lieu of all the money I paid out for said lands, etc., although he expressed himself (page 283, lines 13 and 14 of the evidence) that in all fairness I should have my expenditure but whether he could allow it or not as a matter of law is another matter (and on lines 19, 20 and 21) "I will consider it as he is entitled to whatever I can give him legally" and in delivering judgment said "The case is a hard one and under all the circumstances I think each party should bear his own costs."

That after payment of the $731.20 above mentioned I am still' liable for the sum of $430 being the balance price of said lands, and I submit that it is neither just, fair nor reasonable that I should be put out of my holding and not he allowed the money It cost me, and I feel it in a worse sense than Naboth's Vineyard as in that case the King offered the full value but the Crown has taken mine and robbed me of the price thereof.

That is surely evidence that injustice was done, and that the matter should be looked into. Why should agents or anybody elee take advantage of a few people in a district like that who have invested their life's earnings in these lands anid do not wish to sell them? They could not be considered as real estate subdividers of ten or twenty acre lots, because the land was worth what they paid for it; in some cases it was worth more than they paid for it. My sympathy is, therefore, entirely with those people who have in that matter been treated under conditions that should be investigated.

This amount is required to pay salaries of staff and miscellaneous expenses incident 'to the suspension of construction and the maintenance of work, and also to settle the claims of contractors. There were on this work four large contractors whose claims we had to pay. In, settling their claims, we took over their plant. We are practically reselling that plant, and we shall get the money back for it. That is why we are asking for this appropriation. It is not for the purpose df proceeding with the work.
Has the minister settled with all the contractors?

Of the four contractors there is one, the Dominion Dredging Com-pamy, with whom we have not yet settled. In settling with the different contractors we took over the plants, engines and cars and so- on, that were purchased for this particular work. There is no dispute with the Dominion Dredging Company except that they have a dredging plant and tugs which we did not consider we should purchase because the company had them prior to this work. The amount involved is about $375,000, and there the matter stands. Otherwise, we could have settled with them at any time. Their claim is under consideration with the Government.
I understand that the minister said that the plant that .was taken over was to be disposed of.

A great deal of the plant which the other contractors had came in very useful in connection with the Government railway system and the Canadian Northern Railway system. There were, for instance, engines and cars used for ballasting. The other machinery used in connection with the work we are disposing of to contractors and others, and my assistant chief engineer tells me they are selling it at a profit over the prices paid by the Government.

This will pay the claims that have been disposed! of together with the claim of the Dominion Dredging Company, if we come to a decision in regard to it. This will clean the whole thing up.
