Railways and Canals-chargeable to capital- canals-Trent canal construction, $500,000.

I should like to have the privilege of congratulating the Government on the approaching opening of this splendid work. It is true that only four-fifths of the canal is now completed, but it means the opening of the canal to all that vast arterial commerce of central Ontario upon lake Ontario. The upper part, which *connects with Georgian bay is, of course, not yet finished. It is progressing according to war conditions. That is the best that can be said, and we do not expect anything more, but it will necessarily be completed in a very few years. It is a fine thing to think that this great work, which has been under construction for no less than seventy-eight years, is about to be opened.' It must have been a great proposition, or it would have died a natural death or been slain by criticism many, a long year ago. Of course, in recent years, the population of the country, and of central Ontario, has very considerably increased. The consequence is that, as in all countries where population accumulates, industries have arisen, and favourable opportunities such as exist along the line of the Trent canal are sure to be taken advantage of. Places like Trenton, Campbellford, Peterborough, Lakefield, Lindsay, Fenelon Falls, Orillia, Barrie-all of those places have become centres of industry. The Hydro-Electric has an opportunity of developing 150,000 horsepower. That opportunity has arisen in consequence of this canal.

Is that the available
horse-power?

That will be the available horse-power. The consequence is that you will have a cheap waterway which will immediately serve the interest of no less than 2,000,000 people. More than forty-three constituencies are directly concerned. It is only necessary to quote an instance or two to show how important the opening of this canal is to the whole district to whichlrefer. The Quaker Oats Company have just com-

pleted the reconstruction of their factory in Peterborough. The manager of the firm, from Chicago, told me the other day that the work had cost them $2,250,000, and he assured me that the minute the other end of the canal was opened and they could bring in their grain from the West in their own barges, they would treble this expenditure, and factories! totalling not less than six or seven million dollars would immediately arise. He said the people of Canada, especially in that district, had no idea of what was in contemplation and of the industrial development that must take place as soon as the canal was completed. There are at present 615,000 bushels of oats of the company at Port MicNicoll awaiting transportation. The grain cannot be shipped becaufee of the shortage of cars. Last year, the year before, and on several other occasions this immense factory had to be shut down because they could not get transportation facilities. This great industrial concern is capable of elevating 288,000 bushels of grain a day, and they turn out in one day a hundred cars of their finished product. It is an immense concern, backed by enormous American capital,, and such enterprises as these have sprung up solely because of the Trent cahal. At last we have a very respectable means of conveyance. Right up as far as Peterborough it is eight feet four inches on the sill, and in the course of time we shall have it all the way through. This will enable a long stretch of territory from Peterborough to Lake Ontario to be well served, and the people all the way up to Washago will be able to get by cheap water transportation from Lake Ontario and the waters tributary thereto the goods they need. Therefore, I say I cannot let this milestone in the progress of that district pass-and a milestone also in the progress of Canada for this is a great national undertaking- without directing attention to this great event. On or about 1st June the minister, accompanied by all the members who care to go, will take a boat here at Ottawa, will sail through the Rideau to Kingston, will leave Kingston for Trenton and on up to Peterborough and into the Georgian Bay- the loveliest as well as the most serviceable water route that I know of anywhere in Canada. I am well aware that in the Bast and, needless to say, in the Rockies, there is some beautiful scenery.
Did my hon. friend ever sail around the Bras d'Or lakes?

They are very fine. The hon. gentleman was not quite so appreciative of his own district the other day when he said, speaking on the Civil Service Bill, that composition in Qape Breton was considered decomposition in Ontario.
I did not say that.
The Bras d'Or lakes, the Annapolis valley and many other portions of the East are extremely beautiful.
We do not require canals to beautify the country.

The flowery eloquence of its representatives is enough. In calling attention with my humble voice to the completion, so far as I have outlined it, of this really splendid and important undertaking, let me thank the Government for what it has done. The work has been done under war conditions, which has meant that it has crawled rather than proceeded at the speed we otherwise should have liked to see. I should like further, in the name of that whole district, to invite all hon. gentlemen to accompany the minister on his trip through the canal. The House will then be closed, at any rate until August possibly-I have no authority for saying that, but I fancy it may happen-and I hope all who can will come and see for themselves what I have endeavoured to call attention to, and I can assure them they will be surprised at the importance and greatness of the undertaking to Canada.

I would gather from the remarks of the two hon. gentlemen who have preceded me that this canal passes through their constituencies. I understood that it was the policy of the Government not to	construct	any new

Five hundred thousand dollars is quite an item to expend on a work which is not absolutely essential, and I understand this amount is only a small

All I know is that in our part of the country we only hear about the construction of the canal during an election campaign, when, I understand, the Government always sends out a corps of engineers to make reports and lead the people of the district diredtly to be bene-fitted to believe that some work is actually going to be done. Am I to understand that the inclusion of $500,000 in the estimates for this work is an indication that the Government contemplate an election in the very near future? With regard to the expenditure of large sums of money, I made inquiries the other day as to the cost of piling certain ground in the city of Montreal. Ground was being piled which was not to be used for any building the Government had in contemplation; it was merely piled because the Government were piling, at that time, other ground on which they were going to construct an extension to the examining warehouse in Montreal. What do you think, Mr. Chairman, the piling of this ground cost? You will he surprised to hear it cost close on to $500,000, to be exact, some $470,000, and that was for piling unused ground on which the Government did not know whether it was ever going to erect a building or not. That was a criminal waste of money, during war-time, when we are .paying six to eight per cent interest. We have now before us an item for another $500,000 for a work which I believe could very well stand over until after the war, when we could get the money at a reasonable rate of interest.
Does my hon. friend say that this work has been under construction for seventy-eight years? ,
I said the question of the building of the Trent eanal had been mooted for the past seventy-eight years, according to the hon. member for West Peterborough.

If the jion. gentleman will do- himself the honour of going over to the Chamber of Commerce or the Board of Trade- in his own city and will consult any clerk there, he will get all the data about this canal and will find out that both those bodies in the city of Montreal have again and again strongly endorsed the building of the canal.

He shows how badly he is posted on the needs and wishes of his own city. I am not going to defend this work because it is ancient .history now. The work was dropped for a number of years until 1893 when it was revived and continued until the defeat of the Liberal-Conservative party in 1896. I had the honour of inducing that hon. gentleman to make his first speech in the province of Ontario long years ago, and he did it very nicely. 1 was also partly instrumental in inducing him to make a trip through the charming waters of the Trent system, visiting Peterborough and other towns. He came to the beautiful village of KiflkfieJd in the constituency which I have the honour to represent, and he made one of the most delightful addresses to a vast assemblage there. He told them how this work had been neglected by the great Libeiral-Conservative party and how the great Liberal party had thrown all its energies into it. The people just laughed. That evening my hon. friend was very sad. He and I were sitting holding hands on the deck of the vessel and, in the absence of any one else I endeavoured to console him. He said: " Tell me frankly what happened to-day, that I fell so flat." '1 said:	"'The first thing is that
you read a speech prepared for you by a couple of gentlemen, whom I shall not name. I happened to have an old campaign sheet of the election of 1896 showing a photograph of the spot that he had been sitting on and1 talking and preaching about that day. He appreciated the situation and he realizes the non-sense of the stuff that has been talked by the hon. member sitting at his right to-night. We have a staunch advocate of the Trent canal here in the person of my hon. friend from Maisonneuve.

An item of $500,000 has already been accepted by the House, and another of $57,000. If I remember well it was stated here a few days ago by the minister, when I asked him about going on with works on the St. Charles river in Quebec, that all permanent works would be postponed until after the war.
Yes, and you will save three hundred miles on the journey from Port Arthur to Montreal. .

Yes, and the result is that a number of large towns and cities will have the benefit of water transportation, a thing that they have been looking forward to for many years. Had it not been that they are really nearing completion these works would have been closed down like the others. The result of their being open to navigation within the next thirty days means that vessels will be able to sail from Lake Ontario up to the Georgian bay, thus giving the benefit of transportation to a well settled country. It would hardly have been fair to have closed such works down when it did not involve a very large amount of expenditure.

If I draw attention to these items, it is not in any spirit of opposition. The Government is perfectly justified in continuing works that were started some years ago. But they should adopt the same policy in regard to works that were begun some time ago on the St. Charles river, in Quebec, and for which a contract has been granted. Not only is that the case, but the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden), in 1913, speaking in Quebec, made the declaration that the works on the St. Charles river were of great importance and would be proceeded with. I also think that work in connection with the Transcontinental terminus in Quebec should be continued. The Government have spent millions of dollars on those works, but they have not been touched for a couple of years. Workshops have been erected at a very large cost, but they have not been equipped as was promised in an agreement signed between the Government and the municipal authorities of Quebec. The Government also bought three miles of frontage on the River St. Lawrence at Quebec, for the purpose of the Transcontinental railway, on which they have spent millions. The amount voted in 191718 was $25,000. The department could only have spent $15,000, as there is a revote of $10,000. This year the minister is asking for $57,000. May I ask if conditions have changed now? How does he expect to spend $57,000 this year when he could not spend the whole of his appropriation last year?

Of course, another year has made these conditions referred to very bad, and we really must proceed with the work. There is some dredging along the river that must be done when navigation is proceeded with on and after the first of June.
Welland canal-Heavy repairs, $35,000.

This appropriation is for: (1) renewing three old canal weir foot bridges in concrete, $1,500; (2) replacing four old canal lock gates with reinforced concrete gate bars, $5,000; (3) placing stone protection along certain portions of Summit Level between Thorold and Port Colborne, $15,000;	(4) to clean
out and deepen entrance to Port Dal-house, $6,500;	(5) unforeseen expenditures, $7,000. The bridges to be renewed in item (1) are in a very decayed and unsafe condition. This amount will complete Old Canal weir bridge renewals. Item (2) is a

continuation of work commenced last year, authorized by letter from the chief engineer. With regard to item (3), continued high water and' heavy traffic on the summit level between Thorold and Welland have caused the banks to become badly undermined and eroded. Portions of the towpath, which is the main travelled highway between. Port Eobinson and Welland, have slid into the canal, and immediate rip-rapping is essential to preserve the road. It is estimated that about 9,000 cubic yards of stone protection will be required. No stone protection has been placed on this part of the ' canal since 1914. Item (4) is to be done by contract. Owing to continued abnormally high water in lake Ontario during the past year, it was not found necessary to carry out the work.
Railways and canals-Collection of revenue -Canals-Staff and repairs-Statistical officers, $1,642,500.
Does this vote apply only to canals?

Yes. This amount is required to pay the wages of the staff on all the canals throughout the Dominion. The hon. member will see that last year the vote for staff and repairs was $1,440,000; this year it is $1,600,000. The item for statistical officers, $42,500, remains the same as last year. We have to increase the salaries of the men on the canals staff, and there is an increase in the cost of materials required to keep the canals in repair.
What is the increase over last year?
It is $160,000. It applies to our whole canal system.
What is the increase in wages?

We have not any detailed statement of that increase. The employees are increased from time to time. We intend taking that matter up as soon as the .session is over, and to see that an increase is given to the canal employees throughout the whole system.
Will the increase be uniform for all employees, or will it apply to just a few?
You have to consider each individual class. No uniform system has been adopted1.

The minister might as well give on this item, as on any other, his policy with respect to the patronage system

on the canals of Canada. Last night he told us that he would announce his policy on this matter when he was on his estimates. When he comes to the railway estimates, we shall expect him to tell us his policy with respect to railway patronage. He is now dealing with the canals, where there must be large patronage because a large number of men are employed, and heavy purchases are made. I believe the Government is making an honest attempt to eliminate patronage, but as the railways and canals do not come-as I understand the minister-under the Civil Service Bill, the hand of the minister and of his officers will be upon these matters^ to a greater degree than in other works coming under the Civil Service Act. If the minister is prepared to tell the country what his policy is with respect to matters of that kind, perhaps he can do so on this item.

I think I explained' my policy last night. The hon. member understands that the Railways and Canals Department comes under the Civil Service Bill which is now going through the House; in fact they are now practically under it, as they have been under it since the Order in Council was passed a couple of months ago.
The minister will pardon me: Does he say that the railways and canals come under the Civil Service Act?

No, I do not; I say that the Civil Service Act excepts railways. It does not except employees of the Railways and Canals Department. It does not say that it excepts the employees on the railways and canals. If the hon. member will read the Bill he will see that it excepts employees of the Government railways. So that the canals are under the Civil Service Commission. Since that Order in Council was passed, all appointments in connection with the canals and the other branches of the department, excepting the Government railways, have been made by the Civil Service Commission. For some years purchases in the Railways and Canals Department were made (by the purchasing agent of the department, but they are now made by the War Purchasing Commission. It would be impossible to put the railways under the Civil 'Service Commission, for the reasons which I gave last night.
Under what department are the docks and approaches at Port Borden and Cape Tormentine?

They are under the
direction of the general manager of the Canadian Government Railways at Moncton.
.Mr. JOSEPH READ: Dredging is absolutely necessary there; probably the minister knows it.
Who makes recommendations to the minister for increases to employees on canals?

The Chief Engineer and the Superintendents of Canals go into the matter and make recommendation to me. I have always approved these recommendations; I have no douibt that it will be satisfactory to proceed in that way.
Will the lower-salaried men get larger increases than the higher-salaried men?
That would be taken up when the reports of these officers are made. The larger-salaried men would be statistical officers, and it will (be observed that we have not put in any increases for them.
The increas d cost of living bears more heavily on the man whose salary is from $800 to $1,500 than it does on the higher-salaried man. I would ask the minister to consider this.
The minister has said that the Order in Council of 13th February applies to labourers and employees on the canals. Is that Order in Council being enforced ?	[DOT]
So far as I am aware, it is, in every way.

The Order in Council recites that a doubt existed in the mind of the Prime Minister whether, under the War Measures Act, such an Order in Council could be passed, and that, in the view of Parliamentary counsel and other legal officers of the Government, the Government had no power to pass such an Order. 1 was wondering whether the minister, who wants to stick to the rules so closely, would enforce an Order which was illegal or issued without authority.
A doubt was expressed-
Not a doubt, a certainty.

In the Department of Railways-indeed, in all the departments we have lived up to that Order in Council. In every case the Chief Engineer takes the matter up with the Civil Service Commission. I am trying to live up to that
Order in Council just as if it had been an Act of Parliament.

I desire to corroborate the statement made by the minister with reference to patronage, at any rate, so far as the ship canal at Sault Ste. Marie is concerned. Two vacancies recently occurred in the staff there, and I know that instructions were sent out that applications for appointments to fill these vacancies should be made to the Civil Service Commission. I am glad to hear the minister say that after the work of the Session is over the question of increases to employees of canals will be given consideration. Many of the men employed on these canals are not receiving sufficient salary to maintain their families, particularly in these days of high cost of living.

This year we had before us a Bill to create a bureau of statistics under the Minister of Trade and Commerce. The Department of Agriculture has a statistical branch; so has the Department of Labour. Will the statistics taken m this -case go to the Department of Trade and .Commerce f-or compilation and publication, or is the work of these officers of a special or technical nature?

This name, "statistical officers," applies to men, formerly designated as collectors of canal tolls, who issue passes to vessels going through the canals and obtain particulars as to the destination of the vessels, their cargo, and so on. In this way a record is kept in the department. The name of those officers was changed some years ago and they are now called " statistical officers." One copy of the passes is sent to the department at Ottawa, and in Ottawa are collected the statistics in regard to the vessels passing through the canals. A copy of the passes- and the information obtained by those statistical officers will not be sent to the Department of Trade and Commerce, but the Department of Trade and Commerce will get from the Department of Railways and Canals a detailed statement showing the quantity of grain or any other article of -commerce that the vessels take on board while going through the canals.

How many canals have
we?
Mr. J. D. REI-D:	Eighteen. That, of
course, does not mean only one -collector on each canal. For instance, ^ for the Rideau canal there is a collector in Ottawa for this end, and there is another at Kingston for that end, so that on some of the

canals there is more than one collector. There must also be a night, man. Take for instance the St. Lawrence canals. Vessels are going up and down these canals day .and night, so that there has to he a double staff.
What salaries are allowed to those men?

From $750 to $1,200
a year.

There are eighteen canals which are open for about six months in the year. If we multiply eighteen by two, that would mean thirty-six men employed, say at an average salary of $1,000, or $36,000. As the canals were not numerous, I was wondering, when I saw the amount of the appropriation, whether there was a man at each lock instead of a man at each canal.
Railways and Canals-chargeable to collection of revenue-miscellaneous-Canadian Government railways-compassionate allowance to the widow of the late Harold E Robeson, who died from fatal injuries received in Mulgrave yard on November 4, 1916, $2,000.
'Mr. COPP: I wish to draw the attention of the minister to some correspondence I have had with him in connection with the late Mr. Edmund Cole, who was killed on the Intercolonial railway in February or March last. He was a section foreman on the railway for a number of years-I forget exactly how long-and during the very severe storms of last winter, 11 p.m. when the roads were blocked, he was out assisting in getting trains through. During a very severe storm a train, while going around a curve, struck and killed him. I wrote a letter to .the minister in -connection with the case. Mr. Cole had a small farm. His son is overseas, and his widow is left entirely alone in poor circumstances and with very little *support. While I am glad to see these items in the Estimates, I hope the minister will be able to put an item into the Supplementary Estimates to provide a compassionate allowance for Mrs. Cole.

I am glad the hon. member has mentioned this matter this evening, because the Supplementary Estimates are being considered. I remember the names of at least two men on the Intercolonial in connection with whom compassionate allowances are to he voted. I shall take this matter up to-morrow, and if it has been overlooked I shall then be able to place it in the Supplementary Estimates or give a good reason for not doing so.
[(Mr. J. D. Reid.]

I hope one of the cases for which the minister is asking compassionate allowances is a very touching case, in regard to which I was corresponding with the department, from River Dennis, in the county of Inverness. A young man was killed on the .train there some time last summer. They were filling one of the big cuts at Macdonald Gulch between West Ray road and the Strait of Canso. They were hauling the material from some gravel pit at River Dennis, and they had a long train of gravel cars coming up a heavy grade, to the east of West Bay road.
Was the man's name Campbell?

No, it was McGinnis. A freight train was behind and it began to push the gravel train, and the trains were so long that, when the pressure came upon them, the cars piled up in some way or another and the boy who was working on the train was killed. I wrote the department about the matter. He was an only son, indeed, I think, the only child, a bright young boy of about seventeen years of age. This is a very deserving cas-e, as the minister will see from the correspondence, and something should be done to compensate the father so far as the department can do by the payment of a fair sum of money.

I am glad the hon. member has brought up this matter also to-night, because I shall take it up and see if the father of this young man should receive a compassionate allowance. It strikes me, from looking over the Supplementary Estimates to-day that the name River Dennis is familiar. I am under the impression that we have this man's name on the Supplementary Estimates.
I forget the young man's name, but his father's name is John McGinnis.	.

I shall take the matter up. I was glad to bring in the Bill to provide compensation for Government employees, because the way in which we have been dealing with these matters in the past has not been satisfactory. It is much mo,re satisfactory, in cases of this kind, to he able to deal with them immediately an accident occurs. Now that we have this Act, we shall be able to deal immediately with cases like this instead of having to put the amounts in the estimates.	.

The minister ought to be congratulated on the generous way in which he deals with such cases. In the old days, when, other ministers were handling the department, when I had cases of this kind, I got some money, but I think $750 was the biggest allowance I ever got, and I am. only sorry my people were not killed now instead of ten years ago.
Quebec Bridge, construction, $700,000.
Mr. J. D- EEID: I thought we could take up this item and then perhaps go on to the item for construction on the Quebec and Saguenay railway.
It was not understood that we were going into railway matters to-night.

I understood that some hon. gentlemen wanted to discuss the railways =when these items were called, so I will not press the matter to-night. We could, however, leave one item on which any railway matter could be discussed.
I should like to bring before the committee, if I am in order, the matter of the rate on soft coal from points in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick to points in Quebec.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That could only be done with the unanimous consent of the committee. Discussion of that question would be entirely out of order on this item. Is it the unanimous wish of the committee that the. hon. gentleman shall have the right to speak on the question of soft coal? The hon. gentleman may proceed.

I am informed that for many years the rate of $1.80 per ton prevailed on the Intercolonial for the transport of soft coal from points of origin in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick to points of consumption in Quebec. In the year 1916 the Minister of Railways and Canals almost doubled this rate by raising it to $3.20 per ton. This works a very great hardship to the province of Quebec, because the rate is practically prohibitive. It is more than fifty per cent of the cost of the coal in the lower provinces. We have from the minister's own lips, in reply to questions in the House, information ffom which we can calculate how much it costs the Government railway to carry a ton of coal for the four or five hundred miles between points of origin in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick to points in Quebec. On 18th April last the minister, in reply to a question, told the House that the cost of
transporting a ton of coal for some four hundred miles was $1.65. If we add another hundred miles, which might easily occur between points farther distant from each other, that would add one-fourth to the cost, which would bring the rate to just over $2, to be exact, $2.06. Bjr a curious coincidence if you add 15 per cent to the old rate of $1.80 per ton, you get $2.07, and $2.07 would appear to me to be a fair rate per ton for coal from New Brunswick and Nova Scotia points to points in the province of Quebec. I should like to know whether there is any sound railroad reasop for charging $3.20 per ton to carry coal which must cost a little over $2 per ton? What is the reason that has led the minister to raise the rate that has prevailed for so many years from $1.80 to $3.20 per ton?
Between what points?

I have no exact points, but was taking the minister's statement in reply to a question which appears on page 906 of Hansard this year, and which shows that the cost of transportation from St. Hyacinthe, Montreal, and St. Lambert down to Campbell'ton, a distance of 406 miles, was $1.65. Now to be perfectly fair
i.n my argument I have assumed that there may be another 100 miles between the point of origin of the coal in Nova Scotia or New Brunswick and the point of consumption in the province of Quebec. Therefore, by taking one-fourth of $1.65, we get $2.06, which amounts to the old rate of $1.80 plus 15 per cent. I would take it that it was quite fair for the Minister of Railways to raise the old rate of $1.80 to something over $2 in conformity with the 15 per cent increase which was granted to the other railways, but what I want to be enlightened upon iis why the rates should have been raised from $1.80 per ton to $3.20 per ton, because it is a practically prohibitive rate and shuts out the province of Quebec from the enjoyment of coal from Nova Scotia.
Why does the hon. gentleman say that ia rate of $3.20 from Nova Scotia to Montreal by rail would be prohibitive?

It would add more than fifty per cent to the average price of the coal at the Nova Scotia points where the coal originates. I have some figures here given in answer to questions asked by the Hon. Mr. Tanner in another place. A member of the Government gave these as the average prices for coal charged by the different coal companies in the Maritime provinces:

Acadia Coal Co...	Screened. . .. $6.60	Run of mine. $6.35Nova Scotia Steel	&	Coal	Co	. . . 5.50	5,25Inverness Railway	&	Coal	Co	5.50Bras d'Or Coal Co..	. ... 5.75	5.50I presume that	is	at the mine.	I would
say that a freight rate which represents more than half of the price in most of these instances is a very heavy rate, and extremely heavy when compared with the former rate of $1.80 per ton.

It is hard for me to give the hon. gentleman an answer to the question which he raised without making inquiries as to the reason. The hon. gentleman states that the increase has been from $1.80 to $3.20. When the 15 per cent increase went into effect on the other Toads the rates were increased on the Government railway. I shall make inquiries and be able to answer the hon. gentleman when we take up the estimates again. Three dollars is not a high rate for that haul; I claim it is a low rate. Vessel tonnage is supposed to be carried at a much cheaper rate from Nova Scotia to Montreal than the same tonnage carried by rail. If they were to charge the rates that they are charging now it -would almost make the traffic prohibitive in normal times. The rate to-day from Nova Scotia to Montreal, if we could charter vessels, would amount to at least $3 per ton. Vessel rates have increased very considerably. You cannot get vessels to go from Nova Scotia to Quebec or Montreal.
I would hardly think it fair to compare the rates obtaining today by water with the railway rates, because we all know that the shipping situation is quite abnormal.

I admit that, but we have had to increase the rates on the railways on account of the increased cost of operation. The water rates should not exceed those of the railways. Surely, to bring coal from Nova Scotia to Montreal by rail, the railways should get an amount equal to the vessel rate. The same thing applies to coal which is being transported from Lake Ontario and Lake Erie ports to Montreal. The rate in normal times was about 50 to 75 cents per ton. To-day the rate on coal is about $3.50 per ton from Lake Erie ports to Montreal. That shows the way in which freight rates have been advanced by the vessels. They have also been advanc -d from time to time by the railways. If the 
rates are not raised the railways are going to lose a large amount in the cost of opera-t'on. The hon. member might have read in the press within the last forty-eight hours that the American railways are going to raise their freight rates on account of the high cost of operation. When the 15 per cent increase was ordered by the Board of Railway Commissioners for the other railways the Government railways simply increased their rates 15 per cent the same as the others did. I am not familiar with the whole situation but this little discussion will give me 'an opportunity of becoming thoroughly posted, and when the item comes up again I will be in a better position to give my hon. friend the answer to which he iis entitled.

I know a good deal about this question and perhaps I can throw a little light on it. In ante helium times it did nut cost the Dominion Coal Company more than 35 cents a ton to bring coal from the Cape Breton mines to Montreal. I .am speaking of those large ships that carry
10,000	tons such as the Storstadt. No. railway can compete on a long distance haul with that rate. To-day, with the high cost of ships and the high freights you might send coal from North Sydney, where it originates, to Montreal for $3 ot less. The trouble is that the ships are not available at any price.
Nor are cars, for such a long haul.

Under the present condition of things in regard to the high price of coal for use on the railway, and the high working expenses by reason of increased wages, $3 is not too much from the Cape Breton mines. That is the only place where there is any considerable quantity of coal available. There is some coal shipped from Springhill in Cumberland! county, Nova Scotia, also mined by the Dominion Coal Company, and that is 300 miles nearer Montreal than the Cape Breton mines. No other coal company, except the Pictou Coal Mines, is'producing coal there. They are charging about $6 a ton for coal at the mines to-day, which practically means that the Montreal people, have to take coal from Pictou county laid, down at about $9 as the first cost, regardless of profit, and from Springhill mines the charge would probably be $8.50. I do not know what is going to happen if we have to rely upon the Sydney coal mines,

Until the war broke
out about two million tons of coal per

annum' were (brought from Nova Scotia to Quebec and Montreal !by vessel. In fact that is the only way that coal can profitably be transported to Levis and Montreal; in normal times it wouldi not pay to bring that coal by rail-the railway could not possibly compete with the water rates. Since the outbreak of the war, I do not think there has been any coal brought into Montreal from the Maritime Provinces, the demands of that city for coal having been supplied from the United States. Last year the only coal that came from Nova Scotia to Quebec was brought by two small steamers that the Department of Railways and Canals purchased the year before, vessels of 2,500 or
3,000	tons, respectively, and they altogether carried less than 100,000 tons. This year I do not think we will take any coal from' the Maritime Provinces to Quebec or Montreal -it must all come from the United States, for the reason that no vessels can be secured. The Dominion Coal Company have no- vessels, their fleet having been taken by the British Admiralty. That company lost the Batisea the other day, and have also lost the Louisburg, and they cannot 'get any other vessels; they cannot even take coal to St. John. We are being asked to use the little vessels that we purchased in order to supply the cities of St. John and Halifax. The Intercolonial railway is really taxed beyond its capacity on account of the shortage of cars. The cars are being used to move lumber, pulpwood and other products. If we could only spare the cars it would pay us much better to carry pulp-wood and lumber to the United States, which is profitable, and transport coal from Nova 'Scotia to Montreal in vessels if the necessary ships could ibe obtained.
Is the Quebec bridge open for traffic, and has it been accepted 'by the Government?

The Quebec bridge has been in operation for some months, and I had the opportunity of going over it, 1 think, in November last. Trains are operating backwards and forwards over the bridge, in fact, there is an express'train that runs along the south shore. On the local trains there is a great deal of traffic going to and fro. The good old car ferry Leonard has been disposed of, and we now have the bridge to depend upon.

I would urge upon the minister to have arrangements made with respect to the train from Montreal to the Maritime Provinces so that passengers
travelling to Quebec might cross by the bridge instead of using the ferry.
What the hon. gentleman suggests is that the train should run across the bridge at Quebec and out again?
No, I do not suggest that. A local train might meet the Maritime express somewhere near the bridge, and convey the Quebec passengers direct to that city.
I purpose taking that matter up, but I had intended leaving all such questions until we came to consider the votes for the Government railway systems.
Has the bridge been delivered?

No, it has not been taken off the contractor's hands, because there is some painting and other small things yet to be done. Mr. Montserrat, the chief engineer, tells me that probably the bridge will not be taken over officially until about September. We are responsible, however, for the bridge now.

I am glad that the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Le-mieux) has raised this question, because it is a very important one for the city of Quebec. I hope the minister will give this matteT his attention, so that passengers may be taken to Quebec across the bridge as suggested.

I will take the matter up as promised. Of course, it means an eight or ten mile run from Quebec via the bridge to Levis to meet the train. However, when I am considering the whole railways situation I will take that matter up and see what can be done.
Have any arrangements been made with any of the other roads, except the Quebec lines, with a view to giving them running rights over the Quebec bridge?

No oitheT roads have asked for running rights over the bridge, and until they do so we cannot force them to use the bridge. If other lines want the privilege we will be only too glad to make the necessary arrangements with them.

There are other railway companies that will want to make such an arrangement after the war is over. I can speak for the Delaware and Hudson com-

pany, because I happen to be a director of
the subsidiary companies in Canada. This company had built along the south shore as far as some point in Lotbiniere county [DOT]vhen the first collapse of the bridge took place, and then they stopped work. Then the war came on. I know the company intend to run via the Quebec bridge, but are not in a position to announce their plans until after the war.
. Mr. LAVIIGUEUR: Other railways would like to enter Quebec, but the proper facilities are lacking until the works that have been projected are carried out. That is the pity of it. All the other companies, like the Delaware and Hudson, and the Grand Trunk, would run into the city of Quebec if the required facilities were available.

Opportunity for the further discussion of this matter will be afforded when w'e again go into Supply on the Railway Estimates.
Progress reported.
